mission: Produces a song-as-object prototype: a Raspberry Pi player that recombines the artist's own 8-12 stems by seeded rules so no two plays match, adds an optional local voice line, shows the play number on a Sharp memory LCD, and sits in a printed case with a priced bill of materials (BOM). For a musician with stems and a small listener base. Done means 1,000 logged plays with no duplicate arrangement or clipping, measured battery runtime, a blind test against the studio take, and a pre-sale result above BOM cost.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A generative composer in the Brian Eno / Tristan Perich line would design the variation space before any player code: a stem compatibility matrix (what may sound together, what carries the song's identity), a tempo and key grid every variant respects, and loudness normalized so a sparse arrangement does not sound broken. They would treat the object as a release: boot-to-sound under 20 seconds, survives a yanked battery, plays forever offline. They would get written consent for any cloned voice and run a blind test against the studio master instead of trusting their own ears.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: 1) The multitrack session exported as per-stem WAV, 48 kHz / 24-bit, identical length from bar 1, plus the tempo map. 2) Google's Gemma Translator repository: deployment script, parts list, STL files. 3) Kyutai's Pocket TTS repository and model card: hardware targets, licence, cloning terms. 4) The datasheet for the exact Sharp memory LCD ordered (for example LS027B7DH01) and Adafruit's driver source. 5) Tristan Perich's notes on 1-Bit Symphony. 6) Pi Zero 2 W and Pi 5 power specifications.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Python on Raspberry Pi OS Lite; numpy, soundfile and sounddevice for mixing and gapless output; pyloudnorm for EBU R128 loudness with a -1 dBTP true-peak target; rubberband for tempo drift without pitch change; numpy Generator(PCG64) seeded from device serial plus play counter; SHA-256 of the arrangement JSON as the uniqueness key; atomic counter writes; raspi-config overlay filesystem for a read-only root; systemd autostart; Adafruit Blinka with the Sharp memory display library; a PN532 NFC breakout; a USB power meter; CadQuery or OpenSCAD to adapt the Gemma Translator STL.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A blind ABX-then-preference test with at least 20 listeners comparing three random device takes against the studio master, scored outside the builder's control. Ten pre-sales from existing listeners at a price at least 2.5x BOM. A scripted 1,000-play soak test log showing zero duplicate arrangement hashes, zero true-peak overs and zero audio underruns. A USB power meter reading that matches the claimed runtime within 10%.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: I want to release one song as an offline object that plays a different arrangement every time. Act as a generative composer and embedded engineer. Read the raw sources first: my stems, the Gemma Translator repo, Kyutai's Pocket TTS model card, a Sharp memory LCD datasheet. Then: (1) build a stem compatibility matrix and a variation grammar (order, mutes, tempo drift within +/-3%, fixed key) and justify every rule musically; (2) write a Python player for Pi Zero 2 W and Pi 5 that renders a seeded arrangement, normalizes to -14 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and logs a SHA-256 of every arrangement; (3) test whether Pocket TTS runs fast enough on each Pi, and if not, fall back to a pre-rendered bank of voice lines; (4) drive a Sharp memory LCD showing play number and today's arrangement; (5) adapt the Gemma Translator case and price a 10-unit BOM. Prove it with a 1,000-play soak log, measured battery runtime and a blind test against the studio master. List every claim you could not verify. Clone no voice without written consent.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a generative-music engineer building a one-song hardware edition: a Raspberry Pi object that performs the artist's own stems in a different arrangement each play, with no network. You are skeptical of every speed and size claim in the source posts and you measure instead of repeating them.

CONTEXT
- Precedent: Tristan Perich's 1-Bit Symphony, a composition shipped as a chip in a CD case. Code is the score; the object is the release.
- Hardware recipe: Google's Gemma Translator runs Moonshine, Gemma and a TTS voice offline on a Pi 5 at about 7 tokens per second; the repo ships code, parts list, deployment script and STL case.
- Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS, claimed 100M parameters, local voice cloning, 6x real time, one-command setup, on a desktop, not a Pi.
- Display: Sharp memory LCDs hold pixel state, near e-paper power, about 50 fps on the Playdate.
- NFC stickers as one-tap triggers (byjackprice); the Y-Pan's open CAD plus BOM as product proof; khaen drones as recombination-safe material; Gould's humming as a signature artifact.
- User inputs: 8-12 stems, a target price, which Pi boards they own.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Offline at runtime. No API calls, no telemetry.
- Every arrangement is reproducible from (device_id, play_number) and logged as a SHA-256 of its JSON.
- Integrated loudness -14 LUFS +/-1, true peak at or below -1 dBTP, for every render.
- Tempo drift limited to +/-3% and pitch never shifted.
- Voice cloning only of the artist's own voice with written consent stored in the repo; check the Pocket TTS licence before shipping.
- The SD card must survive a yanked battery: read-only root, counter written atomically.

DELIVERABLES, IN ORDER
1. claims.md: each creator claim with its test.
2. grammar.yaml: stem roles, compatibility matrix, mute, order and tempo rules, a musical reason per rule.
3. player/: Python package with render(seed), play(), tests and a systemd unit.
4. bench.md: render time, boot-to-sound, current draw, Pocket TTS real-time factor, per Pi.
5. voice/: on-device TTS or a pre-rendered bank of 50+ lines selected by seed.
6. display/ and nfc/: memory LCD showing play number and arrangement glyph; NFC tags mapped to moods.
7. case/ plus BOM.csv at quantity 10 and minimum price at 2.5x BOM.
8. soak_report.md: 1,000 renders, hash uniqueness, loudness, underruns.
9. listening_protocol.md: blind test, 20+ listeners, against the studio master.

GAP ANALYSIS (BUILT IN)
Write gaps.md: claim or requirement, status (verified / unverified / false), evidence. Cover at least Pocket TTS speed on the actual Pi, whether it can sing, Zero 2 W RAM headroom with 12 stems, STL fit for your DAC and speaker, the LCD VCOM toggle, and rights to stems and voice. Fill what you can by measurement now; for the rest name the missing hardware or permission.

SELF-QUESTIONS BEFORE STOPPING
- Does the sparsest legal arrangement sound like the song or like a fault?
- Can different seeds sound identical despite different hashes?
- Does any rule run out of variety by play 10,000?
- Is the variation audible in the first 20 seconds?
- Would a fan pay the computed price, and what is the evidence?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if the stems are not time-aligned, if no consent exists for voice cloning, or if the minimum price exceeds the user's target by more than 50%. Otherwise stop when all nine deliverables exist and gaps.md is complete.

RETURN FORMAT
A short summary table: deliverable, path, status. Then the bench numbers, the soak results, the minimum price, and the top five open gaps from gaps.md.

steps.title: Ground truth: stems, repos, claims
steps.goal: Inventory the raw material and turn every creator claim into a test.
steps.prompt:
You are preparing a generative hardware edition of one song. Do not write player code yet.
1. Inspect the stem folder the user provides. For each WAV report sample rate, bit depth, channels, duration in samples, peak dBFS and integrated LUFS (pyloudnorm). Fail the step if lengths differ by more than one sample or sample rates differ; ask the user for a re-export instead of resampling silently.
2. Clone the Gemma Translator repository Google published. Record the exact parts list, the deployment script's model downloads and sizes, and the STL file names and bounding boxes (use trimesh to print extents in mm).
3. Read Kyutai's Pocket TTS repository and model card. Record licence, supported hardware, whether voice cloning needs a reference clip and how long, and whether singing is supported at all.
4. Fetch the datasheet for the Sharp memory LCD you plan to use and note resolution, interface (SPI), the VCOM/EXTCOMIN toggle requirement and current draw.
5. Write claims.md quoting each creator claim with a test: '~7 tokens a second' (Gemma Translator), '6 times faster than real time ... literally one command' (Pocket TTS), 'up to 50 frames per second' (memory display), 'about $100 ... in a week' (Y-Pan cost benchmark).
steps.expect: stems_report.csv with one row per stem, repo_notes.md for Gemma Translator and Pocket TTS, display_notes.md, claims.md with at least 6 claims each paired with a concrete test.
steps.audit: Recompute LUFS on two random stems to confirm the report. Every claim needs a numeric pass/fail threshold. If the Pocket TTS licence forbids commercial use or says nothing about ARM, mark the voice layer at-risk now.

steps.title: Variation grammar
steps.goal: Define the musical rules that make every arrangement different and still the song.
steps.prompt:
Using stems_report.csv, write grammar.yaml for this song.
- Assign each stem a role: identity (must always play, for example lead vocal or main hook), structural (drums, bass), colour (pads, drones, effects), ornament.
- Write a compatibility matrix: pairs that clash (two competing leads), pairs that must co-occur (a kick and its sub layer).
- Define section order rules using the session's bar markers: which sections may be repeated, dropped or swapped, and which order is fixed (the ending stays the ending).
- Define a tempo drift range no wider than +/-3% and forbid pitch change.
- If the song has drone or chord material, treat it like a khaen: sustained free-reed layers that can enter and leave without breaking harmony; give them wider mute probability.
- Add one 'signature artifact' rule in the spirit of Glenn Gould's humming: a quiet, varying human element (a breath, a count-in, a studio murmur stem) that appears in some plays and becomes the edition's fingerprint.
For every rule write a one-line musical reason. Then compute the size of the arrangement space by brute-force enumeration or a combinatorial formula and report it. Target at least 10,000 distinct legal arrangements.
steps.expect: grammar.yaml with roles, matrix, order rules, tempo range and reasons; space_size.md giving the count and the method used.
steps.audit: Table the 20 sparsest legal arrangements. Any missing an identity stem or holding a clash pair means the grammar is wrong; fix and re-count. Under 10,000, loosen ornament rules first.

steps.title: Seeded player and soak test
steps.goal: Ship a deterministic, gapless, loudness-safe renderer with no ML.
steps.prompt:
Write a Python package player/ that implements the grammar from grammar.yaml.
- render(device_id: str, play_number: int) -> (np.ndarray, dict): seeds numpy.random.Generator(PCG64) from SHA-256 of f'{device_id}:{play_number}', samples a legal arrangement, mixes stems in float32, applies tempo drift with the rubberband CLI or pyrubberband, normalizes to -14 LUFS with pyloudnorm, applies a true-peak limiter to -1 dBTP, and returns audio plus the arrangement dict.
- arrangement_hash = SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the arrangement dict.
- play(): reads the counter from /data/counter (atomic write: temp file, fsync, rename), renders, streams to sounddevice with a block size that does not underrun, increments the counter only after playback starts.
- Log one JSON line per play: play_number, hash, LUFS, true peak, render_ms, underruns.
- tests/: determinism (same inputs give byte-identical output), grammar legality on 500 random seeds, counter survives a simulated crash mid-write.
Then run a soak: render plays 1-1000 without audio output and write soak_report.md with duplicate hash count, LUFS min/max, true-peak max and render time p50/p95.
steps.expect: player/ package with passing pytest, soak.log of 1,000 lines, soak_report.md showing 0 duplicates, LUFS within -15 to -13, true peak at or below -1.0 dBTP.
steps.audit: Run pytest and paste the summary. Grep soak.log for any true peak above -1.0 or LUFS outside range; any hit fails the step. Listen to plays 1, 2, 500 and the sparsest seed found; if two sound identical by ear despite different hashes, add a perceptual distance rule (minimum number of changed stems between consecutive plays).

steps.title: Pi bench and power budget
steps.goal: Measure the player on real hardware and pick the board.
steps.prompt:
Deploy player/ to Raspberry Pi OS Lite on each board you have (Pi Zero 2 W, Pi 5). Use a systemd unit with Restart=on-failure and enable the overlay filesystem via raspi-config so the root is read-only, with a small writable /data partition for the counter.
Measure and write bench.md:
- boot-to-first-sound in seconds (phone stopwatch, 5 runs, median)
- render time for a full arrangement, p50 and p95 over 20 plays
- peak RSS memory with all stems loaded (use /usr/bin/time -v); on the Zero 2 W's 512 MB, test whether stems must be streamed from disk instead of held in RAM
- current draw at idle, during render and during playback with a USB power meter, then runtime estimates for the battery in the Gemma Translator parts list
- audio path: I2S DAC HAT or USB DAC, checked with a recorded 1 kHz tone for hum
If render time exceeds the first section's length, pre-render the next play in the background.
steps.expect: bench.md with a table per board, a recommended board and audio path.
steps.audit: Pull power during playback 10 times; any SD corruption or counter reset fails. Compute runtime from measured mA, not marketing capacity.

steps.title: Voice layer: on-device or pre-rendered
steps.goal: Add a variable spoken or sung line without breaking the offline promise.
steps.prompt:
Get written consent from the artist for cloning their voice and store it as consent.md. Install Kyutai Pocket TTS on the chosen Pi following its own README, and measure real-time factor for a 10-second line at the default settings. Compare against the claim of 6x faster than real time.
- If RTF is at or below 0.5 on the Pi, integrate on-device generation: a text grammar of 20-50 fragments (dates, play number, lines from the lyric sheet) assembled by the same seed, synthesized during the previous play.
- If RTF is worse, or the board runs out of RAM, pre-render a bank of at least 50 voice lines on a desktop with the same model and ship them as WAV, selected by seed.
- Pocket TTS is a speech model. Test singing explicitly; if it cannot hold pitch, use speech only, or record the artist singing short variants instead.
Place the voice by grammar rule (for example over the intro drone), duck colour stems 3 dB under it, re-normalize.
steps.expect: voice/ (on-device integration or WAV bank), voice_bench.md with measured RTF, consent.md.
steps.audit: Any of 10 placements that clips, cuts mid-word or masks the identity stem fails. Re-run the soak with voice on.

steps.title: Display, NFC and case
steps.goal: Make the object legible and touchable, and price it.
steps.prompt:
Display: wire the Sharp memory LCD over SPI, use Adafruit Blinka with adafruit-circuitpython-sharpmemorydisplay, and toggle VCOM per the datasheet. Show the play number, the date and a compact glyph of the arrangement (one column per stem, filled if playing). Update only at play start to keep power near zero.
NFC: add a PN532 breakout, read tag UIDs with nfcpy or the Adafruit PN532 library, and map 3-5 tags to grammar presets (mood, movement, 'drone only'). Ship the tags as printed cards.
Case: start from the Gemma Translator STL. Load it in CadQuery or OpenSCAD, add openings for the display, speaker, NFC antenna area and USB-C, and print one test fit. Record print time and filament grams.
BOM: write BOM.csv with part, supplier, quantity-10 unit price and URL for every item, packaging included. Compute unit cost and minimum price at 2.5x BOM; compare with the Y-Pan's roughly $100 parts benchmark.
steps.expect: display/ and nfc/ code, case/ source and STL, a test-fit photo, BOM.csv, pricing.md.
steps.audit: Every BOM row needs a live URL and a quantity-10 price. The display must show a fresh play number after 5 power cycles. If the case blocks NFC reads at 1-3 cm, thin the wall and reprint.

steps.title: Validate and write the gap report
steps.goal: Prove the format is more than a curio or kill it honestly.
steps.prompt:
Run the falsifier from the dive: if listeners prefer the fixed studio take every time, or the BOM forces a price above what 10 fans will pay, the format is a curio.
1. Blind listening test: recruit at least 20 listeners. For each, play the studio master and three random device takes in shuffled order, unlabeled. Ask: can you tell which is the studio take (ABX), and which do you prefer. Record raw answers in listening.csv. Report preference share with a binomial confidence interval.
2. Pre-sale: offer 10 units to existing listeners at the price from pricing.md with a clear ship date. Record conversions and the price.
3. Soak: re-run 1,000 plays on the final hardware with voice and display enabled; report duplicates, loudness, underruns and resets.
4. Write gaps.md: each claim verified / unverified / false with evidence, deliverable status, risks ranked by impact. Fix what you can now; list the rest with reasons.
steps.expect: listening.csv and listening_report.md, presale.md, final soak_report.md, gaps.md with a verdict line: product, curio, or needs another iteration.
steps.audit: Verify the listening test was actually blind: the person running playback must not know which file is which, or use a script that shuffles and logs. If fewer than 20 listeners or fewer than 10 pre-sale offers were made, the verdict must read 'inconclusive', not 'product'.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are auditing a finished generative hardware music edition. You did not build it. Read claims.md, grammar.yaml, bench.md, voice_bench.md, BOM.csv, pricing.md, soak_report.md, listening_report.md and presale.md.
1. List every factual claim in those files (speeds, sizes, prices, uniqueness, loudness, runtime, listener preference) as a numbered table.
2. For each, mark verified, unverified or false, and cite the evidence: a log line, a measurement, a URL, a photo. A claim copied from a creator post with no local measurement is unverified.
3. Re-check: Pocket TTS speed on the shipped board; unique hashes in soak.log; true peak at or below -1 dBTP; counter survives power loss; BOM sourced at quantity 10; blind test with 20+ people; voice consent exists.
4. List what a 10-unit run still lacks: spares, shipping, returns, a firmware update path.
5. Rank all gaps by impact on the falsifier (does it change the product-or-curio verdict).
6. Fix the top three now where possible: rerun a measurement, correct a number, add a missing test.
7. Report what you could not fix, why, and who or what would close it.
self_questions: Does the sparsest legal arrangement still read as this song in its first 20 seconds?
Are consecutive plays audibly different, or only hash-different?
Does play 5,000 still differ from play 50?
Did I measure Pocket TTS on the Pi, or did I repeat the 6x-real-time desktop claim?
Can Pocket TTS sing at all, or did I assume it could?
Does the Pi Zero 2 W's 512 MB hold all stems, or must I stream from disk?
Is the memory LCD's VCOM toggle implemented, or will the image degrade over hours?
Do I have written consent for the voice and the right to sell every stem?
Is play one the strongest arrangement, or a random one?
validation_oracles: Twenty or more blind listeners: an ABX and preference test against the studio master, scripted shuffle, results in listening.csv with a binomial confidence interval.
Ten existing listeners: pre-sale conversions at a price of at least 2.5x quantity-10 BOM cost.
The soak script on final hardware: 1,000 plays, zero duplicate arrangement hashes, zero true-peak overs, zero underruns, zero counter resets.
A USB power meter, cross-checked by ffmpeg's ebur128 filter for loudness: runtime within 10% of the box claim, loudness within 0.5 LU of pyloudnorm on 20 renders.
failure_modes: Inaudible variation. Tell: listeners cannot tell device takes apart. Fix: require a minimum number of changed stems between plays and vary section order.
Sparse takes sound broken. Tell: 'missing something'. Fix: identity stems always on; raise the floor on simultaneous stems.
SD corruption on power loss. Tell: counter resets or no boot. Fix: read-only root, atomic counter writes, separate /data.
On-device TTS too slow. Tell: stutter before the voice line. Fix: pre-render a seeded voice bank; still offline.
BOM creep. Tell: minimum price passes what fans pay. Fix: Zero 2 W over Pi 5, no touchscreen, quote at quantity 10.
Rights problem. Tell: a co-writer or session player objects. Fix: written clearance before pre-sale, kept in stems_rights.md.
agent_direction: Start with local stem inspection and the two repositories; no hardware work until the grammar exists and the soak passes on a desktop. Cache stems_report.csv and models/ so reruns do not refetch. After step 3, spawn parallel sub-agents for case-plus-BOM and for the voice benchmark; they share no files. Stop and ask the user when stems are misaligned, when voice consent is missing, when the computed minimum price exceeds their target by more than 50%, or when a hardware measurement needs a device they have not confirmed owning. Never fabricate a bench number; write 'not measured: no device' instead. Return a top-level README.md that links claims.md, grammar.yaml, player/, bench.md, voice/, display/, case/, BOM.csv, pricing.md, soak_report.md, listening_report.md and gaps.md, with a one-line status for each and the final product-or-curio verdict.

mission: Running this system turns one dataset you genuinely own into a machine-first product: a free llms.txt discovery layer, a structured JSON endpoint metered per call with x402 stablecoin micropayments, and the same data exposed as a listed MCP server, with request logging that separates crawlers, agents and humans. It is for a solo builder, starting with the DejaViewed catalog's own derived fields. Done means a 60-day price experiment with a free control arm, a log that shows whether any agent paid, and an honest verdict against the falsifier: free crawls but near-zero paid calls means the demand side does not exist yet.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A data-licensing and API product lead would first answer whether the data is actually yours to sell: the DejaViewed catalog mixes original work (tiers, classifications, deep-dive synthesis, connection maps) with other creators' captions and transcripts, and only the first kind can be sold. They would design the response format for agents (stable IDs, provenance fields, timestamps, a citation string) before thinking about price. They would run the price test as a controlled experiment with a free arm and pre-registered success thresholds, verify bot identity by reverse DNS rather than trusting user-agent strings, and treat payments with testnet first and a capped hot wallet in production.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: 1) The x402 specification and reference implementations in the coinbase/x402 GitHub repository, including the server middleware variants and the facilitator flow. 2) RFC 9110's definition of HTTP 402 Payment Required. 3) The llms.txt proposal at llmstxt.org. 4) The Model Context Protocol specification and the official MCP registry. 5) Published crawler documentation and IP ranges for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended. 6) The Princeton study on sponsored options across 23 models, read in full including the creator's own caveat that it measures susceptibility in a hypothetical deployment. 7) Your own catalog JSON under the DejaViewed site's api/ output and its field-level provenance.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Node with Hono or Express plus the x402 server middleware from the coinbase/x402 repo, or the Python equivalent if one exists in the repo; USDC on Base Sepolia testnet first; an x402-capable client from the same repo to pay your own endpoint end to end; the official MCP TypeScript SDK or the Python mcp package (FastMCP) for the server; JSON Schema for response records; Cloudflare Workers or Pages Functions for hosting with request logs to R2 or D1; reverse-DNS plus forward-confirm verification for crawler IPs; a deterministic hash bucket on client fingerprint for the A/B arms; a weekly scripted probe of Perplexity and ChatGPT answers for 30 fixed queries, recording whether your records are cited and whether the cited page actually contains the claim.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: Settled payments visible on-chain on Base from wallets you do not control. A request log showing verified crawler and agent traffic by arm. The MCP registry listing and at least one third-party agent installing it. A weekly citation probe showing your records appearing in Perplexity or ChatGPT answers, with the cited page checked to contain the answer.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: I want to sell a niche dataset to AI agents rather than humans. Act as a data-licensing product lead. Start from raw sources: the x402 spec and reference code in coinbase/x402, RFC 9110 on HTTP 402, llmstxt.org, the MCP specification and registry, and the crawler documentation for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot. Then: (1) audit my DejaViewed catalog JSON field by field and split what I authored (tiers, classifications, syntheses, connection maps) from what I do not own (creators' captions and transcripts); only the first may be sold; (2) design a citation-ready record schema with stable IDs, provenance and a citation string; (3) ship a free llms.txt plus a summary endpoint, and a richer x402-metered endpoint tested end to end on Base Sepolia; (4) wrap the same data as an MCP server and list it; (5) log every request with verified bot identity; (6) run a 60-day A/B with arms free, 0.1 cent and 1 cent per call, with success thresholds written before launch. Prove it with on-chain settlements from wallets I do not control and a weekly citation probe. Do not use self-assertion SEO tricks, and do not promise revenue.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a data-licensing product lead and backend engineer. Your buyer is an agent that never sees a landing page. You compete on structure, provenance and price, never on manipulation. You treat demand as unproven until a wallet you do not control pays you.

CONTEXT
- x402 revives HTTP 402 Payment Required so an agent pays a stablecoin micropayment per request (alexanderelorenzo's post frames it as a toll booth for scrapers; the framing is hype-heavy, the protocol is real).
- Quality publishers block AI crawlers: wetclaude reports Consumer Reports disallows GPTBot, Google's AI crawler and Common Crawl, about 60% of high-credibility news sites block AI crawlers, and one in six cited sources is AI-written. Clean, permitted data is scarce.
- The Princeton study: 18 of 23 assistants favored a sponsored option, GPT-5.1 surfaced it 94% of the time, and a 'serve the customer only' system prompt barely moved it. Its own caveat: it measured a hypothetical deployment, not live paid placement.
- Headless software and MCP (Chamath on All-In): agents pick tools on speed, cost and accuracy.
- llms.txt got brycenwood.ai's wrap shop recommended by ChatGPT, built in 5 minutes with Claude Code.
- edward.builds shows Google AI Overviews citing a self-asserted LinkedIn claim the same day. That is the low-quality competition, not a tactic to copy.
- only-cli/oc and Agent Reach show agents want compact, permitted access; do not build on block-evasion.
- The first product is the DejaViewed catalog's api/ JSON.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Sell only fields you authored. Creators' captions and transcripts are excluded from paid records; link to the source post instead.
- Testnet (Base Sepolia USDC) until the end-to-end payment test passes 20 times in a row. Production hot wallet holds no more than 50 USD; sweep to cold storage weekly.
- Never log or print private keys; load them from environment at runtime only.
- Respect robots.txt and platform terms for any data you gather.
- No promised revenue anywhere in docs or listings.

DELIVERABLES, IN ORDER
1. rights_audit.md: every field in the catalog JSON, its origin, sellable yes/no.
2. schema/record.schema.json: id, title, tier, class, summary_authored, connections, source_url, updated_at, citation string, licence.
3. llms.txt and llms-full.txt at the site root describing the dataset and pointing to the free and paid endpoints.
4. api/: GET /v1/free/{id} (title, tier, one-line summary, source link) and GET /v1/records?query= behind x402 middleware, with JSON Schema validation in tests.
5. pay_test.md: 20 end-to-end payments on Base Sepolia using the x402 client from the same repo.
6. mcp/: an MCP server exposing search_records and get_record, with paid calls passing through the same x402 gate, and a registry listing.
7. logging: per request timestamp, path, arm, user agent, verified_bot (reverse DNS forward-confirmed), paid, amount, tx hash.
8. experiment.md: arms free / 0.1 cent / 1 cent assigned by hash bucket, 60-day duration, success thresholds written before launch.
9. probe/: a weekly script that asks Perplexity and ChatGPT 30 fixed questions your data answers, records citations, and checks the cited page contains the claim.

GAP ANALYSIS (BUILT IN)
Write gaps.md as you go: which x402 middleware version you used and whether it supports your host; whether any major agent framework ships an x402 client by default; whether crawlers you see can pay at all; which records lack provenance; which bot identities could not be verified. Close what you can by testing; list the rest with the missing input.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- If I remove every field I do not own, is the remaining data still worth paying for?
- Would an agent pick my record over a free AI-written listicle, and on what visible signal?
- Can a crawler that hits 402 do anything except leave?
- Am I counting spoofed user agents as agent demand?
- Is the free arm cannibalizing the paid one, and does that matter for the falsifier?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and ask if the rights audit leaves fewer than 30% of fields sellable, or if testnet payments fail after two fixes. Otherwise stop when all nine deliverables exist and the experiment is live.

RETURN FORMAT
Table of deliverable, path, status; the rights audit summary; pay_test result; the pre-registered thresholds; top five gaps.

steps.title: Ground truth: rights and raw specs
steps.goal: Know exactly what you may sell and how the protocols really work.
steps.prompt:
Do not write server code yet.
1. Load the DejaViewed catalog JSON from the site's api/ output. For every field, record example value, origin (authored by me, derived by my pipeline from my own judgment, or copied from a creator's post), and sellable yes/no. Captions, transcripts, creator handles' bios and thumbnails are not yours; tiers, classes, deep-dive theses, connection maps and your summaries usually are. Write rights_audit.md and the percentage of sellable fields.
2. Clone coinbase/x402. Read the spec document and list: the 402 response body fields, the payment header the client sends, the facilitator's verify and settle steps, supported networks and tokens, and the server middleware packages available for your stack. Quote file paths.
3. Read RFC 9110 section on 402, the llms.txt proposal at llmstxt.org, and the MCP specification's tool and transport sections.
4. Collect official docs and IP verification methods for GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended.
5. Write claims.md testing the dive's inputs: '18 of 23 models favored the sponsored option', '60% of high-credibility news sites block AI crawlers', 'one in six cited sources is AI-written', 'x402 was coded into the internet in 1991 and remained dormant until 2025'. Mark which you can check from primary sources.
steps.expect: rights_audit.md, x402_notes.md with file paths from the repo, bots.md with verification methods, claims.md.
steps.audit: Spot-check 10 catalog records against rights_audit.md: any sellable field containing creator text verbatim fails the audit. If sellable fields are under 30%, stop and report to the user before building.

steps.title: Record schema and free discovery layer
steps.goal: Make the data machine-legible and discoverable for free.
steps.prompt:
Write schema/record.schema.json (JSON Schema 2020-12) for one record: id (stable, never reused), title, tier, class, summary_authored, connections (array of ids with a one-line reason), source_url, updated_at (ISO 8601), licence, and citation (a ready string like 'DejaViewed catalog, record <id>, updated <date>, <url>'). Add a records/ export script that emits only sellable fields from rights_audit.md and validates every record with jsonschema.
Write llms.txt following llmstxt.org: H1 name, a blockquote summary, then sections listing the free endpoint, the paid endpoint with its price, the MCP server, and the licence. Write llms-full.txt with the schema and 5 example records.
Design the response format for agents, borrowing from the only-cli/oc idea: compact, numbered, no HTML, with a total token estimate per response. Measure tokens for a typical response with a tokenizer and keep the free summary under 300 tokens.
steps.expect: schema/, records/ export with 100% validation pass, llms.txt, llms-full.txt, a token budget table.
steps.audit: Run the validator on the full export and paste the pass count. Fetch llms.txt from the deployed preview URL and confirm it is served as text/plain with no redirects. If any record lacks a citation string or updated_at, fail and regenerate.

steps.title: x402-metered endpoint on testnet
steps.goal: Charge per call and prove the payment loop end to end.
steps.prompt:
Implement api/ with the x402 server middleware from coinbase/x402 for your stack (Hono or Express on Cloudflare Workers or Node).
- GET /v1/free/{id}: title, tier, one-line summary, source link. No payment.
- GET /v1/records?query=&limit=: full sellable records, ranked by a simple BM25 over titles and summaries. Protected by x402 with a price set from an env variable.
- The receiving address comes from env. Never print or log keys; check existence only.
Configure Base Sepolia USDC. Write a client script using the x402 client from the same repo that requests /v1/records, receives 402, pays, retries and gets 200. Run it 20 times. Record each tx hash and latency in pay_test.md.
Then write tests: unpaid request returns 402 with a valid body; paid request returns 200 with schema-valid records; a replayed payment header is rejected.
steps.expect: api/ deployed to a preview URL, pay_test.md with 20 successful testnet payments, passing tests.
steps.audit: Look up 3 tx hashes on a Base Sepolia explorer and confirm amount and recipient. Try a replay and an underpayment; either succeeding fails the step. Grep the repo and logs for any private key pattern; any hit is a stop-everything fix.

steps.title: MCP server and listing
steps.goal: Let agents find and call the data as a tool.
steps.prompt:
Build mcp/ with the official MCP TypeScript SDK or the Python mcp package (FastMCP). Expose two tools: search_records(query, limit) and get_record(id). Write tool descriptions an agent will choose on: state the dataset scope, freshness, price per call and that records carry provenance. The server calls your own HTTP API; paid calls go through the x402 client with a per-session spend cap set by the user, defaulting to 10 cents.
Test locally with the MCP Inspector and with Claude Code as a client: install it, ask a question the data answers, confirm the tool is chosen and the answer cites a record id.
Publish to the official MCP registry following its current submission process, and add the server to llms.txt. Log every MCP call through the same request log as the HTTP API, tagged source=mcp.
steps.expect: mcp/ package, an Inspector screenshot or log, a Claude Code transcript showing a cited answer, the registry entry URL.
steps.audit: Ask Claude Code three questions the data does not answer; the tool must return an empty result, not invented records. Confirm the spend cap stops a fourth paid call in a capped session.

steps.title: Logging and bot verification
steps.goal: Tell real agent demand from noise.
steps.prompt:
Add structured logging to every endpoint: timestamp, path, arm, user_agent, client_ip_hash, verified_bot, paid, amount, tx_hash, latency_ms. Store in D1 or R2 on Cloudflare, or SQLite on a VPS.
verified_bot: for user agents claiming GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot or Google-Extended, check the IP against published ranges or do reverse DNS plus forward-confirm. Unverified claims are labelled spoofed.
Assign arms by a stable hash of client fingerprint into free, 0.1 cent and 1 cent, so a repeat client stays in one arm. The free arm still serves full records; it is the control.
Write a daily report script: requests by arm and verified bot, paid calls, revenue, unique payer wallets, 402 bounce rate (402 served with no retry). Hash client IPs with a salted SHA-256; never store raw IPs beyond verification.
steps.expect: Log schema, a working daily report on preview traffic, arm assignment tests.
steps.audit: Send requests with a forged GPTBot user agent from your own machine; they must be labelled spoofed. Check arm assignment is stable over 100 repeated requests from one client.

steps.title: Experiment and citation probe
steps.goal: Run the 60-day test with thresholds fixed in advance.
steps.prompt:
Write experiment.md before launch: hypothesis, arms, duration 60 days, primary metric (paid calls from distinct wallets you do not control), secondary metrics (402 bounce rate, verified agent requests, citation rate). Pre-register thresholds: for example 'success if at least 25 paid calls from at least 5 distinct external wallets in either paid arm; failure if verified agent requests exceed 1,000 and paid calls are under 5'. Do not change thresholds after launch.
Build probe/: 30 fixed questions the catalog answers well (for example 'best open-source tool for X per DejaViewed'). Weekly, query Perplexity and ChatGPT with browsing, record the answer and every cited URL, and check whether the cited page actually contains the claimed answer, following wetclaude's advice to click every citation. Store results by week.
Do not seed self-assertion posts to game AI Overviews; the probe measures organic pickup only.
steps.expect: experiment.md committed with a launch date, probe/ with a baseline week of results.
steps.audit: Confirm experiment.md was committed before the first paid-arm request in the log. Re-run the probe twice in one day; if results differ wildly, record the variance and increase repetitions per question to 3.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Decide whether agents are buyers yet.
steps.prompt:
At day 60, compute: paid calls and revenue per arm, distinct external payer wallets (exclude every wallet you funded), verified agent requests per arm, 402 bounce rate, and citation rate trend from probe/. Verify a sample of 10 settlements on-chain.
Apply the falsifier: plenty of free crawls but close to zero paid calls means the demand side does not exist yet; write the verdict as 'agents buying', 'agents crawling, not paying', or 'no agent traffic'.
Write gaps.md: every claim from claims.md marked verified / unverified / false with evidence; which agent frameworks could pay x402 during the window; how many 402 responses went to clients that cannot pay; fields you could not sell; anything in logs you cannot explain. Fix what you can now and list the rest with owners.
steps.expect: results.md with a table per arm, the verdict line, on-chain verification list, gaps.md.
steps.audit: Re-derive paid call counts from raw logs, not from the daily report, and confirm they match. If any counted payer wallet is one you funded, remove it and recompute the verdict.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are auditing an agent-facing data product after a 60-day price experiment. Read rights_audit.md, schema/, llms.txt, api/, pay_test.md, mcp/, the request logs, experiment.md, probe/ results and results.md.
1. Enumerate every claim: fields sellable, payments working, bot traffic volumes, paid calls, revenue, citation pickup, registry listing.
2. Mark each verified, unverified or false with evidence: a log query, a Base explorer tx, a test run.
3. Re-check specifically: no creator caption or transcript text in paid records; thresholds in experiment.md predate launch; payer wallets exclude ones the builder funded; verified_bot uses reverse DNS or published IP ranges; no private key appears in code, logs or history; the free arm served the same records as paid.
4. List missing pieces: terms of service for buyers, a refund path, rate limiting, uptime monitoring, a data freshness policy.
5. Rank gaps by whether they could flip the verdict.
6. Fix the top three now.
7. Report what you could not fix and why.
self_questions: Which catalog fields did I author, and which did I copy from creators' posts?
Is the sellable remainder worth more than the free summary to an agent?
Can any mainstream agent client pay x402 today without custom setup, and which ones did I test?
Am I counting spoofed GPTBot or ClaudeBot user agents as demand?
Did I fix the success thresholds before the first paid request?
Is the 0.1 cent arm actually payable given facilitator minimums and gas?
Does my MCP tool description make an agent choose it over a free web search?
Do the citations in the probe actually contain the claim, or is it post-hoc citation?
Is my hot wallet capped and swept, and is the key only ever loaded from environment?
validation_oracles: The Base blockchain: settled USDC payments to the receiving address from wallets the builder never funded, checked on a public explorer.
Cloudflare or server logs: verified crawler and agent requests by arm, with reverse-DNS confirmation.
The MCP registry: a live listing plus an outside client's call in the logs.
Perplexity and ChatGPT: weekly citation probe results showing the catalog cited, with the cited page confirmed to contain the answer.
The x402 reference client from coinbase/x402: 20 consecutive successful testnet payments and a rejected replay.
failure_modes: Selling data you do not own. Tell: paid records contain creators' captions or transcripts. Fix: rebuild the export from rights_audit.md sellable fields only and link to sources.

Bots cannot pay. Tell: high 402 bounce rate and zero retries with payment headers. Fix: keep the free summary rich enough to be cited and log it as the discovery funnel; record the verdict as 'crawling, not paying'.
Spoofed bot traffic inflates demand. Tell: many 'GPTBot' requests from residential IPs. Fix: reverse DNS plus forward-confirm, and report only verified counts.
Micro-price below payment floor. Tell: 0.1 cent payments fail or cost more in fees than they earn. Fix: check facilitator minimums on testnet and adjust the lowest arm or batch credits.
Moving the goalposts. Tell: thresholds edited mid-experiment. Fix: commit experiment.md before launch and audit its git history.
Key leak. Tell: a private key pattern appears in a repo, log or error page. Fix: rotate immediately, move to env-only loading, add a pre-commit secret scanner.
Ranking on manipulation. Tell: seeding self-assertion posts after weak citation results. Fix: refuse; improve record quality and provenance.
agent_direction: Start with the rights audit and the coinbase/x402 repository; nothing else is worth building if sellable fields are thin. Cache the cloned x402 repo, the crawler IP range files and the schema-validated export. Spawn a sub-agent for the MCP server once the HTTP API passes its tests, and another for the citation probe, since they touch separate directories. Run all payment tests on Base Sepolia; ask the user before any mainnet configuration and before setting the production hot wallet, and never read or print key values. Stop and ask when sellable fields are under 30%, when testnet payments fail twice, or when a platform's terms forbid the data use. Return README.md linking rights_audit.md, schema/, llms.txt, api/, pay_test.md, mcp/, experiment.md, probe/, results.md and gaps.md, each with a one-line status, plus the falsifier verdict once day 60 is reached.

mission: Running this system builds a paper-only research tracker that watches the one variable neocloud GPU debt depends on: hourly GPU rental prices after contracts end, set against token price deflation. It logs daily H100 and B200 rental quotes and the cheapest per-million-token prices for three model tiers, pulls contract and debt maturities from public filings, and produces a monthly one-page note. It is for a reader who wants to read the AI capex stack like a credit analyst. Done means 30+ days of clean logged data, a maturity timeline sourced to filings, and notes scored against a naive no-change forecast. No positions are taken.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A credit analyst would build a cash-flow waterfall for one issuer before forming a view: contracted revenue by year from remaining performance obligations, debt service by facility, and the residual GPU rental assumption needed to cover the tail after contracts end. They would separate collateral value (resale and rental of used GPUs) from off-taker credit (the Meta or Microsoft contract), because the 90-95% advance rate rests on the second, not the first. They would track a price index with documented methodology rather than screenshots, define the falsifier numerically before collecting data, and score their own monthly calls against a naive forecast so they know whether the lens adds anything.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: 1) CoreWeave's 10-K and 10-Qs on SEC EDGAR: debt footnotes for each delayed-draw term loan facility, remaining performance obligations, customer concentration, and the useful-life assumption for GPUs in the accounting policies note. 2) Nebius and IREN annual and interim filings, whichever forms they file. 3) Public GPU marketplace data: the Vast.ai offers API, RunPod and Lambda price pages, SF Compute and other spot markets. 4) OpenRouter's models API with per-token pricing, and its public rankings page for token share. 5) DeepSeek's and Qwen's own pricing and model cards. 6) Modine's filings for data-center revenue and backlog. 7) Fundrise VCX's published NAV for the price-versus-value habit.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Python with requests, pandas and DuckDB or SQLite; a daily scheduled job (cron, a systemd timer or a scheduled agent) writing append-only rows with source URL and retrieval timestamp; the Vast.ai CLI or API filtered by GPU model, verified hosts and on-demand pricing, reporting median and 25th percentile, not the minimum; GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models for per-token prices; EDGAR full-text search and the XBRL companyfacts API for structured numbers; a debt maturity ladder built by hand from footnotes and cross-checked to the face of the balance sheet; a simple residual-value model (annual rental revenue per GPU after contract end minus power and opex versus remaining debt per GPU); forecast scoring with mean absolute error against a no-change baseline.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The filings themselves: every maturity and RPO figure carries a page reference that a second reader can open. A second independent price source (for example a published H100 rental index if accessible) agreeing in direction with your marketplace median. Twelve monthly notes scored against a naive no-change forecast, showing whether the lens beats it. A reviewer with credit background reading the waterfall and confirming or breaking it.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: I want to understand whether neocloud GPU-backed debt is exposed to falling post-contract GPU rental prices, and whether token price deflation is feeding that. Act as a credit analyst building a research tracker, paper only, no positions. Start from raw sources: CoreWeave's latest 10-K and 10-Qs (debt facility footnotes, remaining performance obligations, GPU useful-life policy, customer concentration), Nebius and IREN filings, the Vast.ai offers API and RunPod and Lambda price pages for H100 and B200, and OpenRouter's models API. Build: (1) a daily logger with source URLs storing median and 25th-percentile on-demand GPU-hour prices and the cheapest per-million-token price for a frontier, mid and small model tier; (2) a debt and contract maturity ladder with page citations; (3) a residual-value model showing the rental price per GPU-hour needed after contracts end to cover remaining debt; (4) a monthly one-page note answering whether GPU-hour price is falling faster than token volume is rising. Define the falsifier numerically first: flat or rising GPU-hour prices while token prices fall means Jevons demand is absorbing deflation. Score each note against a no-change forecast. List every number you could not source.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a structured-credit analyst building a research tracker on AI infrastructure debt. Paper only. You take no positions, recommend no trades and promise no returns. You source every number to a document or an API response with a timestamp.

CONTEXT
- thewallstreetskinny (ex-Morgan Stanley CDO structurer): neoclouds like CoreWeave borrow 90-95% of capex against strong off-takers like Meta; loan, contract and GPU useful life are nearly the same length, so the tail is thin; post-contract hourly GPU rental is the bull case for the debt.
- techno.optimist.prime quoting Friedberg on All-In: token usage flipped from 80/20 closed-to-open to 80/20 open-to-closed in 12 weeks. Likely sourced from a router's traffic, which is not the whole market.
- gigaqian: DeepSeek V4 Flash re-post-trained, Terminal Bench 2.1 from 61.8 to 82.7, at $0.28 per million output tokens; Qwen 3.8 27B fits about 17 GB at 4-bit on one 24 GB card, benchmarks vendor-reported.
- duck.tate: a $200 Claude Max plan is claimed worth over $7,000 per month of API usage, a third-party estimate.
- natestav: Nvidia's closed-loop cooling still needs chillers; Modine's data-center revenue hit $1.1B, up 73%, with a hyperscaler prepayment. Physical infrastructure with order books is a different bet.
- linalikesmoney: Fundrise VCX at about 25x NAV. The habit: compare price to underlying value.
- atlasberry008: public SaaS down sharply, Atlassian -63%, HubSpot -48%, Workday -47%.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Paper only. If the user later wants to act, the gate is: 12 monthly notes scored, the lens beating the no-change forecast on at least 8, and an outside reviewer signing off; even then no position above 1% of investable capital and a predefined stop. State this gate in the README.
- Every row stores source URL and retrieval time. Never back-fill prices from memory.
- Report median and 25th percentile, never the single cheapest listing.
- Vendor benchmarks and creator figures are claims until checked.

DELIVERABLES, IN ORDER
1. claims.md: each creator figure above with its primary source or 'not found'.
2. logger/: daily job storing GPU-hour prices for H100 SXM, H100 PCIe and B200 from at least three marketplaces, and per-million-token input and output prices for a frontier, mid and small tier from OpenRouter, into DuckDB.
3. filings/ladder.csv: for CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, each debt facility, amount, rate, maturity, collateral, plus contracted revenue (RPO) by expected recognition period, with filing and page reference.
4. model/residual.py: per GPU, remaining debt after contract end versus rental revenue at a given post-contract price, power and opex; output the break-even GPU-hour price.
5. note_template.md and the first note: is GPU-hour price falling faster than token volume is rising, chart of rental price against contract roll-off dates, falsifier status.
6. scoring.csv: each month's directional call versus a no-change baseline.

GAP ANALYSIS (BUILT IN)
Keep gaps.md current: which prices are list prices versus clearing prices; whether marketplace supply is representative of contract renewals at scale; whether token volume data covers enterprise direct API usage; which filings omit maturities by facility; whether GPU useful life in the accounting note matches the 'nearly the same length' claim. Fill what you can from filings and APIs today.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- What post-contract GPU-hour price makes the tail whole, and how far is today's median from it?
- Is marketplace spot pricing a valid proxy for a five-year renewal by a hyperscaler?
- Does falling per-token price mean falling GPU revenue, or more tokens per GPU-hour?
- Is the 80/20 open-weight flip measured on a biased sample?
- Which number in the note would change my conclusion if it were off by 20%?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if a marketplace API requires terms you cannot accept, or if filings do not disclose maturities. Otherwise stop when the logger has run 3 days cleanly and the first note is written; the tracker then continues on schedule.

RETURN FORMAT
Table of deliverable, path, status; the break-even GPU-hour price per issuer with its inputs; today's medians; falsifier status; top five gaps.

steps.title: Ground truth: filings and price sources
steps.goal: Replace creator figures with primary documents and live price sources.
steps.prompt:
Paper research only; no trading advice.
1. From SEC EDGAR, download CoreWeave's most recent 10-K and the latest 10-Q. Extract: each debt facility (name, amount drawn, rate, maturity, collateral, advance rate if stated), remaining performance obligations and the expected recognition schedule, customer concentration (largest customers' share of revenue), and the useful-life assumption for GPUs from the property and equipment policy note. Cite page numbers.
2. Do the same for Nebius and IREN using whatever forms they file.
3. Identify price sources: Vast.ai offers API (filter by GPU name and verified hosts), RunPod and Lambda public price pages, at least one more spot marketplace. Record the exact request or page and whether terms allow automated collection.
4. Call GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models and list prompt and completion prices for a frontier, mid and small tier; pick specific model ids and freeze them.
5. Write claims.md for: '90-95% advance rates', 'loan, contract and GPU life nearly the same length', '80/20 open versus closed in 12 weeks', '$0.28 per million output tokens for DeepSeek V4 Flash', '$200 Max worth over $7,000 of API', 'Modine data center revenue $1.1B, +73%'. Mark each sourced, contradicted or not found.
steps.expect: filings/notes.md with page-cited extracts per issuer, sources.md with request specs and terms status, claims.md.
steps.audit: Re-open 3 cited pages and confirm the numbers match. Any extract without a page reference is removed. If the useful-life policy differs from contract length by more than two years, flag that the 'thin tail' claim may not hold for this issuer.

steps.title: Daily price logger
steps.goal: Log GPU-hour and token prices into one table every day.
steps.prompt:
Build logger/ in Python.
- gpu_prices: for H100 SXM, H100 PCIe and B200 from each source in sources.md, store timestamp_utc, source, gpu, offer_count, median_usd_hr, p25_usd_hr, on_demand or interruptible, url. From Vast.ai, compute stats across verified, on-demand offers, normalized per GPU. From page-based sources, parse listed prices and store as list prices with a flag.
- token_prices: for the frozen OpenRouter model ids, store timestamp_utc, model_id, tier, prompt_usd_per_m, completion_usd_per_m, and the cheapest provider if exposed.
- token_share: if OpenRouter's rankings or another public dataset gives open versus closed token share, store it weekly with its source and note the sampling bias.
Write to DuckDB at data/capex.duckdb, append-only. Schedule daily with a systemd timer or cron at a fixed UTC hour. Add retries with backoff and an error row on failure instead of a silent gap. Respect robots.txt and each site's terms; skip any source that forbids automated access.
steps.expect: logger/ with tests, a scheduled job, at least 3 days of rows per source, an errors view.
steps.audit: Compare one day's Vast.ai median against a manual look at the site; a mismatch over 10% fails. Check there are no duplicate rows per source per day and no null prices without an error row.

steps.title: Maturity ladder and contract roll-off
steps.goal: Map when debt and contracts end, per issuer.
steps.prompt:
From filings/notes.md build filings/ladder.csv with one row per facility: issuer, facility, principal, rate, maturity_date, amortization, collateral, guarantor or off-taker linkage, source_page. Build filings/rpo.csv: issuer, period, contracted_revenue, source_page.
Plot with matplotlib: stacked debt maturities by quarter and contracted revenue by period on the same time axis, one chart per issuer, saved as PNG. Mark the period when large contracts roll off.
Where filings give only aggregate figures, write the assumption you made to split them and mark the row 'estimated'. Do not invent a facility-level schedule that the filings do not support.
Add a customer-concentration column: the share of RPO tied to the largest off-takers named or described in the filing. The structurer's point is that the 90-95% advance rate rests on off-taker credit, so concentration tells you whose credit the lender really holds. Note any facility whose collateral includes the customer contract itself, not just the GPUs.
steps.expect: ladder.csv, rpo.csv, one PNG per issuer, assumptions.md.
steps.audit: Sum principal by issuer and reconcile to total debt on the balance sheet within 2%; a larger gap means a missed facility. Every 'estimated' row must appear in assumptions.md.

steps.title: Residual value and break-even price
steps.goal: Compute the post-contract GPU-hour price the tail depends on.
steps.prompt:
Write model/residual.py. Inputs per issuer: GPUs financed (from filings or capex divided by an all-in cost per GPU you source), debt remaining at contract end, remaining useful life after contract end, utilization assumption, power cost per GPU-hour (GPU TDP plus overhead times PUE times electricity price), and opex per GPU-hour.
Output: break-even post-contract rental price per GPU-hour needed to repay remaining debt over the remaining life, and a sensitivity table across utilization 40-90% and remaining life 0-3 years.
Compare the break-even with today's logged median and p25 from gpu_prices. State the gap in dollars and percent.
Link to token deflation: compute tokens per GPU-hour for a reference open model at a published throughput, multiply by the cheapest per-token price, and show the revenue per GPU-hour an inference seller can earn at today's token prices.
steps.expect: residual.py with tests, a sensitivity table per issuer, a short write-up comparing break-even to market.
steps.audit: Hand-calculate one cell of the sensitivity table and match the code. If any input has no source, label the output 'illustrative' in large text. Check units: dollars per GPU-hour, not per server-hour.

steps.title: Monthly note with a scored call
steps.goal: Write one page a month that can be wrong in a measurable way.
steps.prompt:
Write note_template.md with fixed sections: data window; GPU-hour median and p25 change month over month per GPU; cheapest token price change per tier; token share change with the source's bias stated; break-even gap per issuer; falsifier status; one directional call for next month (GPU-hour median up, flat within 3%, or down) with a confidence.
The falsifier, defined now: if GPU-hour rental prices hold flat or rise while token prices fall over a 3-month window, usage growth is absorbing deflation and the tail-risk thesis is wrong. Compute it from the database, not by eye.
Contrast section: compare Modine's backlog and data-center revenue trend with GPU-hour rental, to keep physical infrastructure with order books separate from rental exposure.
Add scoring.csv: month, call, outcome, naive no-change call, outcome. Paper only: no tickers to buy or sell.
steps.expect: note_template.md, the first note as notes/YYYY-MM.md, scoring.csv with the first row.
steps.audit: Every number in the note must be reproducible by a query saved in notes/queries.sql. If the note contains a trade recommendation or a return figure for a position, remove it.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Check the tracker's numbers and the thesis against outside evidence.
steps.prompt:
1. Re-verify 10 random filing numbers against EDGAR pages.
2. Compare your Vast.ai and RunPod medians with a second independent source, such as a published H100 rental index if you can access one; report direction agreement over the logged window.
3. Check whether any issuer has disclosed contract renewals or re-pricing; that is the true post-contract price and outranks marketplace spot.
4. Score all monthly calls against the no-change baseline. With fewer than 12 months, say the lens is unproven.
5. State the action gate plainly: no positions unless 12 notes exist, the lens beat no-change in at least 8, and a reviewer with credit background signed off; even then no position above 1% of investable capital with a predefined loss limit. Paper tracking continues until then.
6. Write gaps.md: every claim in claims.md marked verified, unverified or false with evidence; list representativeness problems (spot versus contract, router sample versus total token volume); unsourced inputs to residual.py; missing issuers. Fix what you can now.
steps.expect: validation.md, updated scoring.csv, gaps.md with ranked gaps and a falsifier status line.
steps.audit: If any validation step was skipped for lack of access, it must be listed in gaps.md as unverified, not omitted. Confirm no row of gpu_prices was edited after insertion by checking row counts against logs.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are auditing a paper-only AI infrastructure credit tracker you did not build. Read claims.md, sources.md, logger/, data/capex.duckdb, filings/ladder.csv, rpo.csv, assumptions.md, model/residual.py, the notes and scoring.csv.
1. List every numeric claim in the notes and README.
2. Mark each verified, unverified or false, with evidence: a filing page, a query result, an API response timestamp.
3. Re-check: principal in ladder.csv reconciles to the balance sheet; GPU useful-life policy is quoted, not assumed; GPU prices are medians and p25 from verified on-demand offers, not minimums; the token-share series names its sample; residual.py inputs each have a source or are labelled illustrative; no note contains a trade recommendation.
4. List missing pieces: issuers not covered, contract renewal disclosures, power price sources, B200 data depth.
5. Rank gaps by whether they change the break-even gap sign or the falsifier status.
6. Fix the top three now.
7. Report what you could not fix and why, and confirm the no-positions gate is stated in the README.
self_questions: What break-even post-contract GPU-hour price did I compute, and how far is today's median from it?
Is marketplace spot pricing a fair proxy for a hyperscaler renewal on a multi-year contract?
Did I quote the GPU useful-life policy from the filing or assume it?
Does my token-share series come from a router that over-samples hobbyist and open-weight traffic?

DELIVERABLES, IN ORDER
1. claims.md: each creator claim, with replicated / not replicated / untested.
2. overnight/: code and report for SPY and QQQ, 2 years and full history, gross and at 1, 2 and 5 bps per side, with a placebo leg, an out-of-sample split, Newey-West t-stats and a leg-compounding check.

ROLE AND STANCE
You are a legged-robotics researcher running a controlled comparison on a small open robot. You assume the reward will be exploited and that human motion may not fit a duck-shaped body. You measure feasibility before training.

CONTEXT
- summerr.exe trains Pollen Robotics' open-source Microduck to stand: a reward for target body height, 4,096 parallel simulated robots, PPO updating the policy. The result 'stands' in an unintended way: classic reward hacking.
- marc.kaz: FreeMoCap turns ordinary webcams into markerless 3D motion capture with 500+ body, hand and face landmarks per frame, open source, with Blender, Unity and Unreal export.
- HY-Motion 1.0 from Tencent Hunyuan: billion-parameter text-to-motion, 200+ action types, trained on 700 hours of mocap, works on human and robot skeletons, free on Hugging Face.
- ianhubertz: Blender rigid bodies, hinge and spring constraints and motor constraints driven by custom properties, useful for previewing motion physically.
- ppf-contact-solver from ZOZO: GPU contact simulation for soft and cloth contact, relevant if the robot wears a costume or skin.
- s_sapphire_robotics: a running robot that self-stabilizes mechanically with no sensors; design the body first.
- miselyum.art: an animatronic eye sculpture as the target use: motion that reads as intent.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Use the repo's own sim and trainer; do not swap frameworks without a reason written down.
- Retargeted reference must respect joint limits and velocity limits from the robot description; clip and report violations.
- Same seeds, env count, training steps and domain randomization for both arms.
- 3 seeds per arm minimum.
- Hardware deployment only after sim survival above 95% over 100 episodes with randomization.

1. baseline/: reproduced reward-hack run with video and a one-paragraph description of the exploit.
2. reference/: the FreeMoCap or HY-Motion clip, the raw landmark or skeleton file, and the retargeted joint trajectory at the sim's control rate.
3. feasibility.md: joint-limit violations, max joint velocity versus motor limit, and a physics playback in sim or Blender showing whether the motion is dynamically plausible.
4. reward/: the imitation term (phase-conditioned exp of negative squared joint error, plus root orientation and foot contact terms) and its weight, added to the existing reward.
5. runs/: reward-only and reward-plus-imitation, 3 seeds each, with configs and logs.
6. eval.md: joint-tracking RMSE, foot slip, survival, energy proxy, and a blind 'looks intentional' rating by 10+ viewers.
