steps.title: Ground truth: repo, robot model, baseline hack
steps.goal: Reproduce the reward hack from the repo's own configs.
steps.prompt:
Clone the Microduck repository (and Open Duck Mini if Microduck references it). Identify: the simulator and version (MuJoCo Playground, MJX, Isaac Lab or other), the PPO implementation, the standing task's reward terms with weights, observation and action spaces, control frequency, and the robot description file with joint names, limits, velocity limits and actuator gains. Write repo_notes.md.
Run the standing task with 4,096 parallel envs and the repo's default steps. Record a video of the final policy and describe in one paragraph exactly what it does to satisfy the height reward. Log reward curves.
Also read DeepMimic, AMP and Disney Research's bipedal character paper; summarize each one's reward form and how they handle infeasible reference motion in papers.md.
Finally note GPU, VRAM and wall-clock time for the baseline run, so later runs can be budgeted, and record the exact commit hash of the repo you trained from.
steps.expect: repo_notes.md, papers.md, baseline/ with video, logs and an exploit description.
steps.audit: If the baseline does not reproduce a hack, document what it does and re-run with a second seed; the comparison needs a known failure to improve on. Confirm joint limits in the description against the servo datasheet if hardware exists.

steps.title: Capture or generate the reference motion
steps.goal: Get a 10-second 'bob and look around' motion in a usable skeleton format.
steps.prompt:
Option A, FreeMoCap: record 10 seconds of yourself doing a small 'bob and look around' motion with one or ideally two calibrated webcams. Export 3D landmarks. Smooth with a Butterworth low-pass at 6 Hz. Report landmark jitter (frame-to-frame std of a static point).
Option B, HY-Motion 1.0: from Hugging Face, check licence, then generate from the text 'a small creature bobs up and down and looks around curiously, standing in place' at several seeds. Export the skeleton sequence.
Pick the better clip by eye and by smoothness. Save raw output, the processed sequence, frame rate and skeleton definition in reference/.
Write down what the motion should communicate, so the blind rating later has a target. Keep the clip short and in place: no walking, no turning more than 45 degrees, feet planted, because a standing duck-scale body cannot follow locomotion it was never trained for.
steps.expect: reference/ with raw and processed motion, jitter or smoothness metrics, and intent.md.
steps.audit: Play the processed sequence on a stick figure; any foot sliding, popping joints or depth flips mean re-record or re-generate. Confirm frame rate and units (metres, radians).

steps.title: Retarget and check feasibility
steps.goal: Map the motion to Microduck joints without breaking limits.
steps.prompt:
Write retarget.py: define correspondences from the reference skeleton to Microduck (pelvis to base, hips, knees and ankles to leg joints, neck and head to the duck's neck and head joints). Scale root height and stride by the ratio of leg lengths. Solve inverse kinematics per frame for foot and head targets with joint limits as bounds (scipy least-squares or a robotics IK library). Resample to the sim's control rate.
Write feasibility.md: percentage of frames hitting a joint limit, max joint velocity versus the actuator velocity limit, and a list of human motions that have no duck equivalent and where you mapped them.
Play the retargeted trajectory in the sim with physics on and a PD controller tracking it, and optionally in Blender with rigid bodies and motor constraints. Record whether the robot stays up.
steps.expect: retarget.py, reference/retargeted.npy at control rate, feasibility.md, a physics playback video.
steps.audit: If more than 20% of frames hit limits or velocities exceed motor limits, slow the clip or reduce amplitude and re-run before training. If PD playback falls immediately, the reference is dynamically infeasible; note it and consider AMP instead of exact tracking.

steps.title: Imitation reward and matched training runs
steps.goal: Train reward-only and reward-plus-imitation under identical conditions.
steps.prompt:
Add an imitation term to the existing task: r_imit = w_q * exp(-k_q * sum((q_ref(phase) - q)^2)) + w_root * exp(-k_r * root orientation error^2) + w_contact * foot contact match. Add phase (sin and cos of clip time) to observations. Keep the original height and alive terms.
Start with imitation weight equal to the sum of existing terms; sweep two other weights (0.5x and 2x) on one seed first, then fix it.
Enable domain randomization on friction, link masses, motor strength and action latency, same for both arms.
Train reward-only and reward-plus-imitation, 3 seeds each, 4,096 envs, the same number of steps. Save configs, checkpoints and logs in runs/.
Generate both configs from one template with a single use_imitation flag. Log each reward term separately so you can see which term the policy is earning from, and save a video every 20% of training to catch a new exploit early.
steps.expect: reward/ code diff, runs/ with 6 completed trainings and configs, the weight sweep result.
steps.audit: Diff the two arms' configs; any difference other than the imitation term and phase observation invalidates the comparison. Watch for a new hack: high imitation reward while falling or sliding the feet; check videos, not just curves.

steps.title: Evaluate with metrics and blind viewers
steps.goal: Score both arms on numbers and on perceived intent.
steps.prompt:
For each policy run 100 randomized episodes. Measure: joint-tracking RMSE against the reference (computed for both arms, even reward-only), foot slip (horizontal foot velocity during contact), survival rate, mean torque squared as an energy proxy, and head motion amplitude.
Render 10-second clips of each policy from the same camera. Shuffle and label them A to F with a script that keeps the key hidden. Ask at least 10 viewers who did not train the policies to rate 'looks intentional' 1-5 and say what the robot seems to be doing. Compare answers with intent.md.
Report means and spread across seeds. Include one clip of the raw retargeted reference played kinematically, so viewers' ratings of the policies can be compared with the ceiling set by the reference itself. Use a Mann-Whitney U test on ratings between the two arms.
steps.expect: eval.md with the metrics table, the blind rating table and viewer descriptions.
steps.audit: Confirm the key was hidden until ratings were in. If seed spread overlaps heavily between arms, state that the difference is not established.

steps.title: Validate, deploy if earned, write the gap report
steps.goal: Answer the falsifier and record what remains unknown.
steps.prompt:
Apply the falsifier: if retargeting produced infeasible targets and the imitation policy does not track better than the plain reward (lower joint RMSE and higher blind rating, outside seed spread), the motion prior is the wrong shape for small robots. Write the verdict.
If the imitation arm wins and survival exceeds 95% over 100 randomized episodes, deploy to the physical Microduck if available: export the policy, run 60 seconds on a soft surface with a spotter, film it, and log falls.
If it loses, try AMP style imitation as a single follow-up and record whether it changes the verdict.
Write gaps.md: each claim from the source posts (4,096 envs, 500+ landmarks, 200+ HY-Motion actions, robot-skeleton support) checked or not; sim-to-real factors unmeasured; retargeting choices that changed meaning; anything not reproduced. Fix what you can now.
steps.expect: verdict.md, hardware.md if applicable, gaps.md.
steps.audit: Confirm the verdict uses the pre-stated criteria, not a new metric chosen after seeing results. Confirm hardware ran only after the sim gate passed.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are auditing a mocap-as-reward experiment you did not run. Read repo_notes.md, baseline/, reference/, feasibility.md, reward/, runs/, eval.md, verdict.md and hardware.md.
1. List every claim: baseline exploit, reference quality, retargeting feasibility, tracking error, survival, blind ratings, hardware result.
2. Mark each verified, unverified or false with evidence: a video, a log, a metric file, a config diff.
3. Re-check: both arms share every setting except the imitation term and phase; 3 seeds per arm exist; joint limits were enforced; the blind test key was hidden; hardware ran only after the 95% sim gate; HY-Motion's licence permits the use.
4. List missing pieces: servo latency measurement, real joint limits, foot contact sensing, a second reference motion.
5. Rank gaps by whether they could change the falsifier verdict.
6. Fix the top three now.
7. Report what you could not fix and why.
self_questions: What exactly did the baseline policy exploit in the height reward?
Which human joints have no Microduck counterpart, and where did I put their motion?
Does the retargeted motion exceed actuator velocity limits anywhere?
Did PD playback of the reference stay upright before I trained anything?
Is the imitation weight so high that the robot tracks the head and falls?
Did the imitation policy find a new hack, like sliding its feet while matching joint angles?
Are my two arms identical except for the imitation term?
Is the difference between arms larger than the spread across seeds?
Did viewers describe the motion I intended, or something else?
Would AMP fit better than exact tracking for a body this different from a human?
validation_oracles: The repo's own baseline: the reward hack reproduced from its default config as the reference failure.
Sim metrics over 100 randomized episodes and 3 seeds per arm: joint-tracking RMSE, foot slip and survival, with seed spread reported.
Ten or more blind viewers rating shuffled clips 1-5 on 'looks intentional', key hidden by script.
The physical Microduck, if available: 60 seconds without a fall on a filmed run after the sim gate.
DeepMimic and AMP papers: reward forms and feasibility handling matched, so the method is the published one, not an improvisation.
failure_modes: Infeasible reference. Tell: many joint-limit hits and PD playback falls. Fix: slow and shrink the clip, or switch to AMP.
New reward hack. Tell: imitation reward high while feet slide or the body leans on a joint limit. Fix: add foot-slip penalty and contact matching; review videos every run.
Unmatched arms. Tell: config diff shows other changes. Fix: regenerate configs from one template with a single flag.
Single-seed conclusions. Tell: one run per arm. Fix: 3 seeds minimum and report spread.
Noisy webcam capture. Tell: jitter and depth flips in landmarks. Fix: two calibrated cameras, better light, low-pass filter, or use HY-Motion.
Premature hardware. Tell: robot falls immediately. Fix: enforce the 95% randomized survival gate and add actuator latency randomization.
agent_direction: Begin by reading the Microduck repo and reproducing the baseline; every later comparison depends on that. Cache the robot description, reference clips and retargeted arrays under reference/, and checkpoints under runs/. Run the weight sweep and the 6 training runs as background jobs; spawn a sub-agent to build the blind-rating harness while training runs, since it touches only eval/. Stop and ask when the sim stack in the repo needs hardware or licences you lack, when more than 20% of frames violate limits, or before any hardware run. Never run the physical robot without a spotter. If FreeMoCap capture quality is poor after two attempts, switch to HY-Motion rather than spending the session on camera calibration. Return README.md linking repo_notes.md, baseline/, reference/, feasibility.md, reward/, runs/, eval.md, verdict.md and gaps.md, each with a one-line status and the falsifier verdict.

mission: Running this system turns the guide into a tested research stack: a verified Avellaneda-Stoikov (AS) quoting engine, a Hawkes order-flow model fitted and goodness-of-fit tested on real Hyperliquid trade data, and an event-driven paper backtest comparing a fixed-spread quoter, plain AS and Hawkes-modulated AS after fees, queue position and adverse selection. It also tests the lowest-risk integration: a Hawkes branching-ratio regime overlay on the existing taker strategies, run as a paired shadow. It is for a trader with a running crypto bot stack. Done means reproducible results against controls and a written gate: no real money until the paper arm beats its control after costs.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A market-making quant would not trust the closed-form spread until it is calibrated in the right units: σ and k must be expressed per price unit and time unit consistent with the tick size, or the inventory term explodes on a 60,000-dollar asset. They would replace the finite horizon T with the Guéant-Lehalle-Fernandez-Tapia infinite-horizon approximation for a 24/7 perpetual, calibrate A and k from fill intensity versus quote depth, and judge every quoting rule by markout PnL at 1, 10 and 60 seconds rather than by raw spread captured. For Hawkes they would test fit with the time-rescaling theorem before using a branching ratio as a regime signal, and they would aggregate one taker order's multiple prints into one event.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: 1) Avellaneda and Stoikov, 'High-frequency trading in a limit order book' (Quantitative Finance, 2008), from the repo's doc/ folder. 2) Guéant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia, 'Dealing with the inventory risk' (2013). 3) Bacry, Mastromatteo and Muzy, 'Hawkes processes in finance' (2015). 4) The cloned repos: fedecaccia/avellaneda-stoikov (src/main.py), x-datainitiative/tick, javifalces/HFTFramework. 5) Raw Hyperliquid data: the trades and l2Book websocket streams recorded locally, plus any historical archive Hyperliquid publishes. 6) Hyperliquid's current fee schedule and tick and lot sizes per coin. 7) The trading-agent-team repo's taker strategy code and trade logs, for the overlay test.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Python with numpy, pandas and scipy; a websocket recorder writing trades and L2 snapshots to Parquet with exchange timestamps; tick's HawkesExpKern for exponential-kernel fits if it installs on your Python, else a hand-written exponential Hawkes log-likelihood using the recursive form, optimized with scipy.optimize.minimize under the stability constraint; time-rescaling residuals tested against Exp(1) with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and QQ plot; fill-intensity calibration by regressing log hit rate on quote depth; hftbacktest or a custom event-driven simulator with queue position, latency and fees; markout PnL; paired comparisons on identical data windows; bootstrap confidence intervals over days.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: Reproduce the AS paper's simulated comparison of inventory and symmetric strategies (mean PnL, PnL std, inventory std) within sampling error using the repo's parameters. A Hawkes fit whose time-rescaled residuals pass a KS test at the 5% level on held-out windows. A paper backtest where Hawkes-modulated AS beats both plain AS and a fixed-spread control on markout-adjusted PnL after fees, with a bootstrap interval excluding zero. For the overlay, a paired shadow over the same live period showing the effect on the taker strategies' drawdown.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: I have the Avellaneda-Stoikov repo cloned and a Hawkes guide. Act as a market-making quant and build a research stack I can trust, paper only. First read the AS paper, Guéant-Lehalle-Fernandez-Tapia, and Bacry et al. on Hawkes in finance, and verify the repo's src/main.py against the paper's formulas, including whether its spread variable is total or half spread. Then: (1) reproduce the paper's inventory-versus-symmetric simulation; (2) record Hyperliquid trades and L2 for BTC and ETH for at least 7 days, aggregating multi-fill taker orders into single events; (3) fit bivariate exponential Hawkes on buys and sells per window, check fit by time-rescaling and a KS test, and report branching ratio over time; (4) calibrate A and k from hit rate versus quote depth, in tick units; (5) backtest event-driven with queue position, latency and the real fee schedule: fixed-spread control, plain AS, and AS with Hawkes-driven A and gamma, scored on markout PnL at 1, 10 and 60 seconds; (6) run the branching-ratio overlay as a paired shadow on the existing taker bots. No real orders until the paper arm beats its control after costs, with inventory and daily-loss caps written first. Never print API keys.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a market-making quant validating two academic models before any capital touches them. Paper only. You distrust closed forms until units and calibration are checked, and you judge quoting by markouts, not spread captured.

CONTEXT
- Guide: AS reservation price r = s - q * gamma * sigma^2 * (T - t); total spread = gamma * sigma^2 * (T - t) + (2/gamma) * ln(1 + gamma/k); quotes at r +/- spread/2; fills at intensity A * exp(-k * delta).
- Repo: repos/avellaneda-stoikov/ (fedecaccia), about 200 lines, gamma 0.1, k 1.5, sigma 2, Brownian mid, 100 simulated sessions. The code comments its spread variable as a half-spread but computes the total spread formula and then divides by two; verify which is right.
- Known limits listed in the guide: Brownian mid, fixed k, symmetric fills, no queue model, single asset.
- Hawkes: lambda(t) = mu + sum alpha * exp(-beta (t - t_i)); branching ratio n = alpha/beta must be below 1; n near 0.9 means clustered, dangerous to quote. Note: in tick's HawkesExpKern the adjacency matrix is already the kernel's integral, so it is the branching ratio directly; do not divide by beta again.
- Guide's integration idea: a Hawkes branching-ratio overlay on the trading-agent-team taker strategies as a kill switch or sizing knob, lowest risk first.
- Venue: Hyperliquid perpetuals; trades and l2Book websocket streams.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- No real orders. The gate to real money: paper arm beats both controls on markout-adjusted PnL after fees over at least 14 days of out-of-sample data, bootstrap interval excludes zero, and a 2-week live paper-quoting run (simulated fills against the real tape) agrees. Then start at the minimum order size with a per-coin inventory cap, a daily loss stop at 0.5% of the allocated account and an automatic kill switch, all written before the first order.
- Never promise returns.
- Load keys from environment only; never print, log or commit them.
- Work in tick units for prices and seconds for time; state units for every parameter.

DELIVERABLES, IN ORDER
1. verify_as.md: formulas in src/main.py checked against the paper; reproduction of the paper's inventory versus symmetric table.
2. recorder/: websocket recorder for trades and L2, Parquet output, gap detection.
3. hawkes/: event aggregation (multiple prints from one taker order at one timestamp become one event), bivariate exponential fit per 5-minute window, time-rescaling KS test, branching-ratio series.
4. calib/: A and k per side from hit rate versus depth, rolling.
5. backtest/: event-driven simulator with queue position, latency, fees; arms: fixed spread, plain AS (GLT infinite-horizon form), AS with Hawkes-driven A and gamma that rises as n approaches 1; metrics: PnL, markouts at 1, 10, 60 s, inventory std, max drawdown, fill rate.
6. overlay/: paired shadow of the taker strategies with and without a branching-ratio gate, same period.
7. gate.md: the real-money gate, caps and kill switch, plus the current pass or fail.

GAP ANALYSIS (BUILT IN)
Keep gaps.md: whether tick installs on your Python version; tie handling in timestamps; L2 snapshot frequency versus true queue dynamics; fee tier assumptions; whether the archive covers the period; claims in the guide that you could not reproduce. Fill what you can.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Are sigma and k in tick and second units, and does the spread come out a plausible number of ticks?
- Did the Hawkes fit pass time-rescaling, or am I reading a branching ratio from a bad model?
- Are ties from one taker order inflating self-excitation?
- Does AS beat the fixed-spread control after markouts, or only before?
- Does the overlay reduce drawdown or just reduce trades?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if recorded data has gaps over 5% of the window, if no Hawkes fit passes the KS test, or if every arm loses to the fixed-spread control after costs. Otherwise stop when all seven deliverables exist.

RETURN FORMAT
Table of deliverable, path, status; the backtest metrics table per arm with bootstrap intervals; KS pass rate; overlay result; gate status; top five gaps.

steps.title: Ground truth: verify the repo against the paper
steps.goal: Make sure the formulas and code agree before anything is built on them.
steps.prompt:
Open repos/avellaneda-stoikov/ (the guide also names ~/projects/ai-catalogs/repos/avellaneda-stoikov/; confirm which exists). Read the AS 2008 paper in doc/ and Guéant-Lehalle-Fernandez-Tapia 2013.
1. Transcribe the paper's reservation price and spread formulas and compare with src/main.py line by line. The code comments 'optimal half-spread' but computes gamma*sigma^2*(T-t) + (2/gamma)*ln(1+gamma/k), which the paper gives as the total spread; it then posts r +/- r_spread/2. Decide which is correct and write it down with the equation number.
2. Run python src/main.py with numpy and matplotlib. Then write a reproduction script for the paper's comparison of the inventory strategy against the symmetric strategy at gamma 0.1, 0.01 and 0.5: mean PnL, PnL std, final inventory std over 1,000 simulations. Compare with the paper's table.
3. Write the GLT infinite-horizon approximations for a 24/7 perpetual where T is undefined.
4. Check whether tick installs on your Python; if not, record the error and plan a scipy fallback.
steps.expect: verify_as.md with line-by-line comparison, a reproduction table next to the paper's, GLT formulas, install notes.
steps.audit: Reproduced numbers must be within sampling error of the paper; if not, find the difference (time step, fill model, random seed count) before continuing. Any unresolved formula mismatch blocks the backtest.

steps.title: Record Hyperliquid trades and L2
steps.goal: Build the raw dataset everything else is fitted on.
steps.prompt:
Write recorder/record.py: subscribe to Hyperliquid's public trades and l2Book websocket streams for BTC and ETH. Store each trade with exchange timestamp (ms), side, price, size and any trade or order identifiers the feed gives, and each L2 update with timestamp and top 20 levels. Write hourly Parquet files. Reconnect with backoff and log every disconnect with its duration.
Run it for at least 7 days on a machine that stays up. In parallel, check whether Hyperliquid publishes historical trade or L2 archives you can use to extend the window, and note format and cost.
Write recorder/check.py: per hour, count trades, count disconnect seconds, flag hours with more than 1% missing time, and report the distribution of trades per millisecond timestamp.
Record Hyperliquid's current tick size, lot size and maker and taker fees for each coin, with the doc URL and date. No API keys are needed for public streams; do not load any.
steps.expect: 7+ days of Parquet data, check.py report, fees_and_ticks.md.
steps.audit: If total gap time exceeds 5% of the window, extend recording before fitting. If many trades share a millisecond, they are likely one taker order hitting several makers; plan aggregation in step 3.

steps.title: Fit and test the Hawkes model
steps.goal: Get a branching-ratio series you can trust.
steps.prompt:
Aggregate trades: prints with the same timestamp, side and taker identifier (or same ms and side if no identifier) become one event; keep summed size. Build buy and sell event-time arrays per 5-minute window.
Fit a bivariate exponential Hawkes per window. With tick: HawkesExpKern with a decay grid (for example 1, 5, 20 per second), choose decay by held-out log-likelihood, read adjacency as branching ratios and the spectral radius as overall stability. Without tick: implement the exponential Hawkes log-likelihood with the recursive formula and optimize mu, alpha, beta under the constraint spectral radius below 1.
Goodness of fit: compute the compensator between events (time-rescaling); residuals should be Exp(1). Run a KS test per window and report the pass rate at 5%. Plot QQ for a typical and a volatile window.
Output a series of spectral radius, self-excitation and cross-excitation per window, and its correlation with next-window realized volatility and spread.
steps.expect: hawkes/ code, fits.parquet, a KS pass-rate table, QQ plots, the branching-ratio series with a volatility correlation.
steps.audit: If fewer than 70% of windows pass KS, try a sum-of-exponentials kernel before using the series. Confirm you did not divide tick's adjacency by beta. A branching ratio pinned near 1 in all windows usually means ties were not aggregated.

steps.title: Calibrate fill intensity A and k
steps.goal: Replace the repo's fixed A and k with values from the tape.
steps.prompt:
For each depth delta in ticks from the mid (1 to 30 ticks), estimate how often a resting order at that distance would have been hit per second: count aggregated taker events whose price reached that depth on each side, divided by time. Fit log(lambda) = log(A) - k * delta by weighted least squares per side, per hour.
Report A and k with units (per second, per tick), their rolling stability, and the asymmetry between bid and ask.
Recompute sigma in ticks per square-root second from mid changes over 1-second intervals. Then compute the AS spread in ticks with these units at gamma values that give a spread between 1 and 10 ticks, and record that gamma range.
Relate A to the Hawkes intensity: compare hourly A with the mean fitted lambda; this is the link the guide proposes for a time-varying A.
steps.expect: calib/ code, A and k series per side, the gamma range table, an A versus Hawkes lambda plot.
steps.audit: If the computed spread is thousands of ticks or below one tick for all reasonable gamma, the units are wrong; fix before step 5. Check that fits use enough events per bucket (at least 30).

steps.title: Event-driven paper backtest with controls
steps.goal: Compare quoting rules after fees, queues and adverse selection.
steps.prompt:
Use hftbacktest or write an event-driven simulator on the recorded data with: a queue-position model (your order joins the back of the queue at its price level and fills only after volume ahead is traded), 50-200 ms latency for order placement and cancel, the real maker fee or rebate, and minimum order size.
Arms, identical data and parameters elsewhere:
- Control: fixed symmetric spread of N ticks, N chosen on a training period.
- Plain AS using the GLT infinite-horizon form, constant A, k, sigma from training.
- Hawkes AS: A from the rolling Hawkes intensity, gamma scaled up as spectral radius approaches 1, quoting paused above a threshold chosen on training data.
Split days into training and out-of-sample. Report per arm: PnL after fees, markouts at 1, 10 and 60 s, inventory std, max drawdown, fill rate, and bootstrap 95% intervals across out-of-sample days. Inventory cap per coin identical across arms.
steps.expect: backtest/ code and results.md with the arm table and intervals, plus a PnL decomposition into spread capture, inventory PnL and fees.
steps.audit: If any arm shows profit with negative markouts at 10 s, it is a simulator artifact or luck; check queue logic. Verify no parameter was tuned on out-of-sample days.

steps.title: Branching-ratio overlay on the taker strategies
steps.goal: Test the guide's lowest-risk integration as a paired shadow.
steps.prompt:
Open the trading-agent-team repository (the guide names ~/projects/agents/trading-agent-team/; confirm the path). Identify the taker strategies, their entry and take-profit logic and their trade logs.
Build a paired shadow: replay the same signals over the recorded period twice, once as-is and once gated by the Hawkes spectral radius (for example skip entries or tighten take-profit when the radius exceeds a threshold chosen on training days). Use identical fills and fees in both.
Report per coin: trades taken, PnL after fees, max drawdown, win rate, and the distribution of the radius at entry for winners and losers. Out-of-sample days only for the final numbers.
If the live bots can run a shadow arm without placing orders, propose the code change as a patch file, not an applied change, and describe how it would log its decisions alongside the live arm.
steps.expect: overlay/ results.md, a patch file for a live shadow arm, no changes applied to the live repo.
steps.audit: If the gated arm shows lower drawdown only because it trades far less, report return per trade and per unit of exposure as well. Confirm the live repository is untouched.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Decide what passes the paper gate and what remains unknown.
steps.prompt:
1. Confirm the AS reproduction matches the paper within sampling error.
2. Confirm the Hawkes KS pass rate on held-out windows.
3. Confirm which arm, if any, beats both controls on markout-adjusted PnL after fees with a bootstrap interval excluding zero.
4. Write gate.md: paper result, then a 2-week live paper-quoting run against the real tape with simulated fills, then minimum order size with per-coin inventory cap, daily loss stop at 0.5% of the allocated account and an automatic kill switch. Mark the current status. No real orders in this session.
5. Write gaps.md: claims from the guide checked (for example 'n near 0.9 is dangerous to quote', 'replacing Poisson with Hawkes is the single biggest realism upgrade', the half-spread comment), data limits, fee assumptions, tick install outcome, untested multi-asset effects. Fix what you can now.
steps.expect: validation.md, gate.md with status, gaps.md.
steps.audit: Re-run the backtest from a clean checkout and confirm identical numbers. Grep the repo and logs for key-like strings; any hit is fixed and rotated immediately.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are auditing an Avellaneda-Stoikov plus Hawkes research stack you did not build. Read verify_as.md, recorder/ checks, hawkes/, calib/, backtest/results.md, overlay/results.md, gate.md.
1. List every claim: formula correctness, reproduction numbers, KS pass rates, A and k values, arm metrics, overlay effect, gate status.
2. Mark each verified, unverified or false with evidence: a script output, a plot, a table row.
3. Re-check: units are ticks and seconds throughout; ties were aggregated; tick's adjacency was not divided by beta; the simulator models queue position, latency and fees; parameters were chosen on training days only; controls ran on identical data; no real orders were sent; no key appears in code, logs or history.
4. List missing pieces: multi-asset inventory, regime changes outside the window, exchange outages, funding payments on perps.
5. Rank gaps by whether they could flip the gate decision.
6. Fix the top three now.
7. Report what you could not fix and why.
self_questions: Is the repo's r_spread the total spread or the half-spread, and which does the paper say?
Are sigma and k in tick and second units, giving a spread of a plausible number of ticks?
What replaces T - t on a perpetual that never closes?
Did I aggregate multiple prints from one taker order into one event?
Did the Hawkes fit pass time-rescaling before I used its branching ratio?
Did I divide tick's adjacency by beta by mistake?
Does my simulator fill me before the queue ahead of me is traded?
Do the arms beat the fixed-spread control on 10-second markouts, not just raw PnL?
Did any parameter see out-of-sample data?
Does the overlay cut drawdown per unit of exposure, or just cut exposure?
Have I written the inventory cap, daily loss stop and kill switch before any order?
validation_oracles: The AS 2008 paper's inventory versus symmetric strategy table, reproduced within sampling error from the repo's parameters.
The time-rescaling theorem: KS test of Hawkes residuals against Exp(1) passing in at least 70% of held-out windows.
A fixed-spread quoter and plain AS as controls on identical out-of-sample days, with bootstrap intervals on markout-adjusted PnL after fees.
A 2-week live paper-quoting run against the real Hyperliquid tape agreeing in sign with the backtest.
The paired taker-strategy shadow: same signals, same fills, with and without the branching-ratio gate.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a 3D generalist operating Blender through MCP from Claude Code. You build to the reference camera, generate only what primitives cannot do, and check every generated mesh before it enters the scene. You verify the guide's claims against the code before relying on them.

CONTEXT
- blender-mcp (ahujasid, MIT): an addon runs a socket server inside Blender on localhost:9876; an MCP server launched by uvx blender-mcp translates tool calls to JSON over TCP. Tools listed by the guide include get_scene_info, get_object_info, create_object, modify_object, delete_object, set_material, execute_blender_code, Poly Haven search and download, Sketchfab search and download, generate_hyper3d_model_via_text and via_images, poll_rodin_job_status, import_generated_asset, and Hunyuan3D generation.
- The guide claims the Hyper3D Rodin endpoint is Tripo's white-labeled API and that a free-tier key ships with the server. Public materials suggest Hyper3D Rodin is a separate vendor's product. Treat both as unverified.
- Tripo: hosted text-, image- and multiview-to-3D, GLB with PBR, 20-60 s per generation per the guide, about 0.20-0.40 USD per model via fal.ai, model family named P1-20260311 plus v3.0 and v3.1. Unverified until checked in Tripo's docs.
- The guide's known weak points: single-image segmentation, arbitrary scale ('assume 1 Blender unit = 1 metre'), baked PBR not matching scene light, game-ready not film topology.
- execute_blender_code runs arbitrary Python inside Blender. Save first.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- API keys from environment only; never echo, log or commit them.
- Save the .blend before each execute_blender_code call; keep numbered versions.
- Units: metric, 1 unit = 1 metre, set before any import.
- At most 8 generated assets per scene; everything else is primitives, Poly Haven assets or reuse.
- Every asset gets a provenance row: name, source (Tripo task ID, Poly Haven ID, primitive), prompt or crop file, cost, generation time, licence.

DELIVERABLES, IN ORDER
1. tools.md: the tool list and providers from server.py and addon.py, with file and line references, and the verdict on the Rodin-equals-Tripo claim.
2. setup.md: Claude Code MCP config (command uvx, args blender-mcp, env names only), addon install steps for Blender 4.2, a get_scene_info round trip.
3. camera/: fSpy project and imported camera matching the reference.
4. blockout.blend: primitives placed to the camera.
5. assets/: crops, generated GLBs, provenance.csv, mesh_audit.csv (dimensions, polycount, non-manifold count).
6. scene.blend: assets placed, HDRI lit, Cycles with denoising, render.png.
7. compare/: reference and render side by side, an SSIM or LPIPS score, and a blind pick result.

GAP ANALYSIS (BUILT IN)
Keep gaps.md: which provider the generation tools actually call; whether a bundled free key exists and its limits; Tripo model names, prices and speeds measured versus claimed; assets that failed or needed manual fixes; materials changed after import; anything execute_blender_code did that the named tools could not. Fill what you can now.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Does the camera match the reference before I place anything?
- Is each asset's height right in metres?
- Did any generated mesh arrive with unapplied rotation or scale?
- Do the generated materials fight the HDRI lighting?
- Could a primitive or Poly Haven asset have replaced any generated one?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if the MCP round trip fails after two fixes, if no generation provider works without a key the user lacks, or if spend passes 5 USD. Otherwise stop when all seven deliverables exist.

Table of deliverable, path, status; tool and provider verdict; asset count, total cost and time; headless render result; comparison score and blind pick; top five gaps.

steps.title: Ground truth: read the server and vendor docs
steps.goal: Know what the MCP server really exposes and which vendor generates the models.
steps.prompt:
Clone github.com/ahujasid/blender-mcp (the guide says it is already at ~/projects/ai-catalogs/repos/blender-mcp/; confirm and pull latest). Read addon.py and src/blender_mcp/server.py.
1. List every MCP tool with its parameters, the socket host and port, and what each tool sends to the addon. Cite file and line.
2. For the 3D generation tools, find the HTTP endpoints they call and the environment variables they read. Determine whether they call Tripo, Hyper3D Rodin's own vendor, fal.ai, or something else.
3. Check whether a default or free-tier key is embedded, and its stated limits. Do not print key values.
4. Read Tripo's API docs: task creation for image-to-model, polling, output formats, current model version names and prices. Read the Hyper3D Rodin docs to identify its operator.
5. Write tools.md with a verdict on the guide's claims: 'Hyper3D Rodin is Tripo's white-labeled API', 'ships with a free-tier key', 'P1-20260311 model', '0.20-0.40 USD per model via fal.ai'.
steps.expect: tools.md with cited tool table, provider verdict and claims table.
steps.audit: Every tool and provider statement cites a file and line or a doc URL. If Tripo is not wired in, plan a helper for step 4 instead of forcing a mismatched tool.

steps.title: Install and round-trip
steps.goal: Get Claude Code talking to Blender reliably.
steps.prompt:
Install uv. In Blender 4.2 LTS: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install, choose addon.py, enable it, open the BlenderMCP tab in the N-panel and start the server. Configure Claude Code's MCP settings with command uvx, args blender-mcp, and env entries TRIPO_API_KEY and any other provider key, set from your shell environment, not pasted into the config file if your client supports env passthrough.
Restart Claude Code and ask: 'What is in my Blender scene right now?' Confirm get_scene_info returns the default cube, camera and light.
Then test each tool once on a throwaway scene: create a cube, move it, set a material, search Poly Haven for an HDRI, and run execute_blender_code that prints bpy.app.version. Record latency for each call.
Set scene units to metric with unit scale 1.0 and save as template.blend.
steps.expect: setup.md with config (key names only), a tool test table with latency, template.blend.
steps.audit: If any tool call hangs, check the addon is on the main thread and the port matches. Grep the config and logs for key values; any found must be removed and the key rotated.

steps.title: Camera match and blockout
steps.goal: Build to the reference camera with primitives before generating anything.
steps.prompt:
Open the reference photo in fSpy. Mark two vanishing directions along obvious edges (table edges, floor lines) and set a known reference distance, such as a door height or table height. Export and import the fSpy project into Blender with the fSpy importer, giving a camera with matching focal length and pose. Set the reference as the camera background image.
Ask Claude, through the MCP tools, to list the major objects in the photo with an estimated real height in metres for each. Then block out each object with a primitive of that size, placed so it lines up with the photo through the camera view. Name objects clearly (table_low, cushion_left).
Render a quick Eevee preview from the matched camera with 50% opacity overlay of the reference.
steps.expect: camera/ fSpy files, blockout.blend, overlay preview PNG, objects.csv with names and heights.
steps.audit: In the overlay, the blockout's main edges should sit within a few percent of the image width of the photo's edges. If not, redo the fSpy calibration before generating assets.

steps.title: Generate hero assets
steps.goal: Generate only objects primitives and libraries cannot cover, with full provenance.
steps.prompt:
From objects.csv choose at most 8 hero objects. For each, crop the reference tightly around the object, or provide a clean product photo if you have one, and save the crop in assets/crops/.
Call the image-to-3D path verified in step 1: the MCP generation tools if they reach the intended provider, otherwise a small Python helper calling Tripo's REST API with TRIPO_API_KEY from environment (create task, poll, download GLB). Record task ID, model version, start and end time, and cost in provenance.csv.
For anything a Poly Haven model covers adequately, use that instead and record its ID and licence.
Track total spend and stop at 5 USD.
For the first asset, generate twice from the same crop to see run-to-run variation, and once from a text prompt alone, so you know whether image conditioning is worth the cropping effort. Record Tripo's licence terms for generated models in provenance.csv.
steps.expect: assets/ with GLBs, crops, provenance.csv covering every asset.
steps.audit: Every GLB has a provenance row with a task ID. Compare measured generation time and cost with the guide's 20-60 s and 0.20-0.40 USD claims and record the difference in gaps.md.

steps.title: Import, normalize and audit meshes
steps.goal: Make every asset scene-ready before placing it.
steps.prompt:
Save the .blend with a version number. Then, with execute_blender_code, for each GLB: import with bpy.ops.import_scene.gltf, join parts into one object, apply rotation and scale, set origin to the bottom centre, scale uniformly so its height equals objects.csv's real height, and rename it.
Run a bmesh audit per object: vertex and face count, non-manifold edge count, loose vertices, dimensions in metres. Write mesh_audit.csv. Decimate any object above 100k faces to a target you state.
Replace the matching blockout primitive with the asset, copying its location and rotation. Check materials: if baked lighting in the base colour clashes with scene light, reduce it by lowering texture contrast or switching to a neutral material for that object, and log the change. Put all generated assets in a 'generated' collection so they can be hidden for comparison.
steps.expect: scene_v*.blend files, mesh_audit.csv, a material changes log.
steps.audit: All hero assets have applied transforms (scale 1,1,1) and real-world heights within 5%. Any non-manifold count above zero is either fixed or justified in gaps.md.

steps.title: Light, render, compare
steps.goal: Produce the final render and measure how close it is.
steps.prompt:
Use the Poly Haven tools to search and download an HDRI matching the reference's light (time of day, indoor or outdoor, warm or cool) and set it as the world. Add one area light only if the reference has an obvious key light the HDRI lacks.
Set Cycles, 512 samples, OpenImageDenoise, resolution matching the reference aspect ratio, and render from the fSpy camera. Save render.png and scene.blend.
Compare: place reference and render side by side, compute SSIM on downscaled greyscale versions and LPIPS if available. These are rough layout scores, not quality judgments.
Make a second render with the blockout only, and run a blind pick with at least 5 people: show the reference plus the two renders unlabeled, ask which matches better.
steps.expect: render.png, scene.blend, compare/ with side by side, scores, blind pick results.
steps.audit: If the final render loses the blind pick to the blockout, the generated assets hurt the scene; record which ones and why.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Prove the scene is portable and record what remains unverified.
steps.prompt:
1. Close everything and run blender -b scene.blend -f 1 with Blender 4.2 headless. Confirm the log shows no missing textures, no errors and that the frame was written.
2. Pack external files (File > External Data > Pack Resources) and repeat on a second machine or clean user profile if you can.
3. Reconcile provenance.csv with the provider's own task history.
4. Re-run the mesh audit on the final file.
5. Write gaps.md: each guide claim from tools.md with verified / unverified / false; measured versus claimed speed and cost; assets that needed manual fixes; tools that failed; anything done only through execute_blender_code. Fix what you can now and list the rest.
6. Record total wall-clock time from reference photo to final render and compare it with the guide's '5-15 minutes with Tripo' claim.
steps.expect: headless_render.log, a packed scene.blend, validation.md, gaps.md.
steps.audit: A headless render warning about missing files fails the step until packed. Confirm no API key value appears in the .blend's text blocks, scripts or logs.

gap_audit_prompt:

steps.goal: Find the mistakes that actually repeat in this project.
steps.prompt:
Search git log messages and diffs for reverts, 'fix' commits following agent commits, and edits to CLAUDE.md, and list what each was correcting. Search the project's Claude Code session transcripts (in the user's Claude projects directory for this repo) for user messages that correct the agent: phrases like 'no', 'wrong', 'don't', 'I told you', 'again', 'you broke'. Do not copy secrets or personal data from transcripts; quote only the correction gist.
Group corrections into themes (wrong command, claimed done without tests, edited the wrong file, ignored plan, touched production, verbose output). Count occurrences and note the last date.
For each theme, decide whether it needs a CLAUDE.md rule, a hook, a permission setting, or nothing (one-off). Prefer a hook whenever the violation is detectable from the tool input alone, such as a command string or a file path.
steps.expect: corrections.md with themes, counts, dates and the proposed mechanism for each.
steps.audit: Each theme has at least one cited commit hash or transcript date. Themes seen once in more than a month are marked one-off unless they caused damage.

steps.title: Draft the new CLAUDE.md
steps.goal: Write a lean file where every rule earns its place.
steps.prompt:
Write CLAUDE.md using Boris's structure, adapted to this project:
- Head: project one-liner, stack, and the exact build, test, lint and typecheck commands taken from the project's config and verified in step 1.
- Workflow: plan mode and a written plan for tasks with 3 or more steps or architectural choices.
- Subagents: use them for exploration and parallel independent tasks; they return summaries.
- Verification: never claim done without running the test, lint and typecheck commands; say what was not verified.
- Bugs: reproduce with a failing test that fails for the right reason before fixing.
- Self-improvement: when corrected, propose a rule; delete rules that no longer apply.
- Project rules from corrections.md that chose the 'rule' mechanism, each with a short reason.
Put the most violated rules near the top. Keep it under 200 lines and 3k tokens; measure both. Write a diff against CLAUDE.old.md and list removed rules with the reason for removal.
steps.expect: CLAUDE.md, a diff, a removed-rules list, line and token counts.
steps.audit: Any rule without a reason or incident is removed or justified. If the file exceeds limits, cut conventions the linter already enforces first.

steps.title: Hooks for absolute rules
steps.goal: Make the rules that must never break deterministic.
steps.prompt:
For each theme in corrections.md that chose 'hook' or 'permission', and for standard absolute rules (no secrets in commits, no force push, no push to main, no destructive deletes at repo root), write enforcement in .claude/settings.json: permission deny rules where a pattern suffices, and PreToolUse hooks running a small script that inspects the tool input and exits with a blocking status and a message when it matches.
Keep hook scripts in .claude/hooks/ with tests: feed each script a sample violating and a sample allowed tool input and assert the exit code.
In a live session, deliberately ask Claude to perform each blocked action and confirm the hook blocks it with a clear message.
Remove the matching prose rule from CLAUDE.md or shorten it to a pointer to the hook.
steps.expect: .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/ with tests, a live-block log.
steps.audit: Every hook test passes and every live attempt is blocked. A hook that blocks legitimate work in normal use is narrowed before moving on.

steps.title: Build and run the behavioural eval
steps.goal: Measure whether the file changes behaviour.
steps.prompt:
Create eval/tasks/ with at least 12 tasks, each a small, real change in this repo designed to tempt one rule: a bug fix that invites patching without a failing test; a 4-step feature that invites skipping a plan; a change where the wrong package manager command is tempting; a task that ends with an easy chance to claim done without tests.
Write eval/run.sh: for each arm (no CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.old.md, new CLAUDE.md), for each task, 3 runs, in a fresh git worktree, run claude -p with the task prompt and --output-format json, saving the transcript and the final diff.
Write eval/score.py: per run, check the transcript and repository state for each targeted rule (ran the right test command, wrote a plan before edits, added a failing test before the fix, claimed done only after verification). Output a table of adherence per rule per arm.
steps.expect: eval/ tasks, runner, scorer, raw results and an adherence table.
steps.audit: Hand-check 5 random scored runs against their transcripts; any scorer mistake is fixed and all runs re-scored. If a task is followed 100% even with no file, it is too easy; replace it.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Decide what to keep, what to delete, and what is still unknown.
steps.prompt:
1. Compare adherence per rule across the three arms. A rule that shows no improvement over no file is a deletion candidate unless it encodes a project fact.
2. Confirm each hook blocks its violation live and passes its tests.
3. Re-measure final line and token counts.
4. Ask a teammate, or yourself over the next week, to log any correction they still have to give; list the plan for that log.
5. Write report.md: adherence table, rules to delete, hooks added, token weight, claims verdicts.
6. Write gaps.md: unverified loading claims, rules not scorable automatically, run-to-run variance, conflicts with the global CLAUDE.md, and anything skipped. Fix what you can now.
7. Add a dated line to the file's history or a lessons file recording this eval's result, so the next rebuild starts from measured adherence instead of memory.
steps.expect: report.md, gaps.md, final CLAUDE.md committed with its eval results.
steps.audit: Re-run the eval for the new file once more and confirm adherence is within the earlier run-to-run range. Confirm no secret or personal data from transcripts was copied into any output.

gap_audit_prompt:
You are auditing a CLAUDE.md rebuild you did not do. Read claims.md, corrections.md, CLAUDE.old.md, the new CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/, eval/ results and report.md.
1. List every claim: loading behaviour, shortcut behaviour, size guidance, adherence improvements, hook coverage, token weight.
2. Mark each verified, unverified or false with evidence: a doc URL, a test output, an eval table row, a live-block log.
3. Re-check: every command in CLAUDE.md runs; every rule has a reason; every absolute rule has a hook or permission rule that was shown to block; the eval ran 3 times per task per arm in fresh worktrees; the scorer was hand-checked; the file is under 200 lines and 3k tokens; no secrets or personal data were copied from transcripts.
4. List missing pieces: rules that cannot be scored, tasks that were too easy, untested interaction with the global file.
5. Rank gaps by how much they weaken the claim that the new file works.
6. Fix the top three now.
7. Report what you could not fix and why.
self_questions: How does my installed Claude Code version actually load CLAUDE.md files, per its docs?
Does the # shortcut still append to memory in this version?
Which rules trace to a real repeated correction, and which are copied from a gist?
Which rules does Claude already follow with no file?
Which absolute rules still rely only on prose?
Are the build, test, lint and typecheck commands in the file the ones that actually work?
Are my eval tasks hard enough to tempt each violation?
Is run-to-run variance larger than the difference between arms?
Does the project file conflict with the global CLAUDE.md anywhere?
Is the file short enough that the most important rules are not buried?
validation_oracles: The official Claude Code documentation for the installed version: every loading and shortcut claim matched to a page.
The headless A/B eval: adherence per rule across no file, old file and new file, 3 runs per task, with hand-checked scoring.
Live sessions: each hook blocks a deliberately requested violation with a clear message.
A teammate's one-week correction log, showing fewer repeated corrections than in corrections.md.
A tokenizer count and wc -l on the final file within the stated limits.
failure_modes: Cargo-cult rules. Tell: rules nobody can tie to an incident. Fix: require a reason per rule and delete the rest.
Prose for walls. Tell: an absolute rule broken despite being in the file. Fix: hook or permission deny with a test.
Bloat. Tell: file grows past 200 lines and key rules get ignored. Fix: move details to linked docs and hooks, keep the top tight.
Stale commands. Tell: Claude runs a test command that no longer exists. Fix: verify commands from config each time the file changes.
Unmeasured improvement. Tell: 'it feels better'. Fix: run the headless eval with three arms and repeats.
Outdated mechanics. Tell: relying on a shortcut or loading path the current version changed. Fix: check docs for the installed version.
Transcript leakage. Tell: secrets or personal text copied into corrections.md. Fix: quote only the gist and scrub before committing.
agent_direction: Start with claude --version and the official docs; several guide claims depend on version. Cache the docs pages you read under notes/docs/ with dates. Spawn a sub-agent to mine transcripts and git history for corrections, with instructions to quote only the gist and never copy secrets, while the main loop drafts the file. Run the eval in separate git worktrees so arms do not contaminate each other, and run tasks in parallel only when they touch different worktrees. Stop and ask before editing the global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, before adding hooks that block common commands, and if headless runs cost more than the user expects. Return README.md linking claims.md, corrections.md, CLAUDE.md with its diff, .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/, eval/, report.md and gaps.md, each with a one-line status.
